item.title: Stereoselective Synthesis and Skeletal Rearrangements of Iodinated Azabicyclohexanes: Access to Densely Functionalized [2.2.1] and [3.1.0] Heterobicyclic Scaffolds
item.description: An optimized method for intramolecular iodoamination of cyclobutenyl methanamines is reported. This stereospecific reaction gives densely functionalized, diastereomerically pure 2-aza-5-iodobicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes in moderate to high yields. Reactivity of the iodo group is explored, including anionic, radical, and cationic mechanistic pathways. Radical reduction replaces the iodo group with hydrogen, while nucleophilic substitution using AgOAc results in retention of configuration. Skeletal remodeling via cation rearrangements gives [3.1.0] and [2.2.0] bicyclics, providing a pathway to multiple saturated heterocycles.

item.title: Article title Minimal Complexity Freeze-Drying Setup for Ultralow-Density Aerogels
item.description: Aerogels are among the world’s lightest known solid materials, appreciated for their high porosity and excellent insulation capabilities. However, standard production methods such as sol-gel chemistry combined with supercritical drying tend to be complex, expensive, and often impractical in small-scale laboratory contexts. This article introduces a minimal complexity and cost-effective setup for producing polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) aerogels, utilizing a freeze-drying technique rather than supercritical drying. The setup is built using accessible hardware and eliminates the need for high-pressure equipment or hazardous chemicals. The article outlines the fabrication protocol and operating principles, and demonstrates the production of lightweight, porous aerogels using pure PVA and PVA together with additives like wool fibers and graphene, as well as a preliminary thermal performance evaluation. By reducing costs and complexity, this open-source hardware enables broader experimentation with aerogel composites synthesized through freeze-drying, making production more accessible to researchers and engineers.

item.title: Unlocking Structurally Diverse Initiators for Controlled Radical Polymerizations
item.description: Directly initiating well-controlled radical polymerizations from common functional groups is a key strategy for synthesizing advanced polymer architectures. Carboxylic acids are one of the most abundant functional groups and are therefore advantageous to use for polymer grafting; however, the α-carbon of most carboxylic acids are not stabilized by radical stabilizing groups. There are few examples of initiating controlled radical polymerization from unstabilized carbon-centered radicals, and the resulting polymers have poorer initiator efficiencies and higher Ð than desired. Herein, we report a general strategy for initiating two dominant methods of controlled radical polymerization, ATRP and RAFT, from the α-carbon of redox activated carboxylic acids. This method successfully grafts from a wide array of unstabilized and stabilized carbon-centered radicals with excellent molar mass agreement, narrow Ð, and incredibly high chain-end fidelities, opening the door for advanced grafting applications that are inaccessible through current methods.

item.title: A Gauge-Invariant Aromaticity Scale from the Loop Holonomy of the One-Body Density Matrix
item.description: This work establishes an aromaticity scale based on the one-body reduced density matrix (1-RDM). The fundamental quantity is defined as the product of normalised coherence links along a closed loop, referred to as the loop holonomy. This quantity is invariant under local phase redefinitions; its modulus CN and phase ΦN form two gauge-invariant scalars that measure the coherence strength and the phase sign of the loop, respectively. The topological existence of the loop is determined by the cycle rank β1 of the bond graph. The framework extends naturally to polycyclic systems (cycle-space holonomy), spherical systems (S2 shell coherence), block and spin degrees of freedom, degenerate and fractionally occupied situations, multireference methods (CASSCF/CASCI), and excited states (Baird’s rule).

item.title: Does low interfacial resistance guarantee high critical current density? A quantitative review of sodium-metal/NASICON interfaces
item.description: Solid-state sodium batteries with NASICON-type solid electrolytes (Na3Zr2Si2PO12) are promising for large-scale energy storage. Their development is limited by two challenges at the sodium metal/electrolyte interface. The first is a high interfacial resistance. It arises from the point contacts between the two solids, the poor wetting of NASICON by sodium and a poorly conducting contamination layer formed in air. The second is the penetration of sodium dendrites through the electrolyte, which causes a short circuit and is quantified by the critical current density (CCD). Many strategies, such as surface treatments, interlayers and composite anodes, reduce the interfacial resistance, and a lower resistance is commonly expected to give a higher CCD. This review explains both challenges and summarises these strategies. To examine how far they suppress dendrite penetration, we collected the interfacial resistance and the CCD of 122 cells reported in 49 papers. Among the cells with an interfacial resistance below 30 Ω cm2, 25 of 37 reached a CCD of 1 mA cm−2. Only 10 of 85 cells above this value did, and none of the 27 cells above 300 Ω cm2. Nevertheless, a low interfacial resistance was not sufficient for a high CCD, and several cells reached a high CCD at a moderate resistance. We therefore discuss other factors that limit the CCD, namely void formation during stripping, the electronic conductivity of the electrolyte and defects in its microstructure, and the strategies that address them, such as doping, sintering aids and densification. Finally, perspectives for future research are provided.

item.title: Design and development of smart molecular imaging probes for theranostic imaging
item.description: To review the recent progress in smart molecular imaging probes in theranostics with the emphasis on stimuli-responsive activation, multimodal innovation, and their potential application. Smart probes, and especially enzyme-activated and stimuli-responsive nanoplatforms, pave the way to high-contrast, specific imaging and therapy by activating them on-site- avoiding off-target effects and leading to enhanced diagnostic accuracy and treatment follow-ups. Systematic evaluations of studies were done in enzyme-responsive-fluorescence, redox-activatable MRI, and multimodal nanoprobes that have the combination of modalities like PET/MRI, optical/MRI, and photoacoustic imaging. Particular significance was put into such design strategies as enzymatic self-assembly, microfluidic synthesis, and automated radiosynthesis methods. Smart probes had an increased specificity and retention in diseased tissues. Particularly, organic fluorescent probes catalyzed by enzymes had high imaging signals in the tumor and inflammation areas, whereas magnetic nanoprobes with redox responsivity had a high T1/T2 contrast enhancement, regulatory perishability Moreover, multimodal imaging platforms permitted precise anatomical, functional as well as molecular imaging on preclinical disease models. The preclinical performance of stimuli-responsive smart probes has been impressive, overcoming the shortfalls in precision, high-contrast imaging and theranostics capabilities. The next steps must focus on scalable synthesis, strong safety testing, and analytic analysis implementation using AI to bring these innovations to personalized care of patients to the full extent.

item.title: Average Sulfur Rank-Driven Material Responses in Polymers
item.description: Elemental sulfur is an abundant but underutilized petroleum refining byproduct. Although sulfurcontaining polymers offer distinctive material properties, they are commonly described by their overall sulfur content, rather than number of consecutively bonded sulfur atoms. This article reports a stepgrowth polymerization method for producing sulfur-containing polymers with systematically varied average sulfur ranks. Average sulfur ranks ranging from 1.0 to 4.2 were determined via elemental analysis, whereas solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance and Raman spectroscopy supported the expected sulfur-rank-dependent structural differences. Varying the average sulfur rank systematically altered the thermal, tensile, and local molecular responses during deformation. In all-solid-state cells, the polymers with varying average sulfur ranks exhibited distinct capacities and cycling characteristics. These results establish average sulfur rank as a molecular design parameter linking the sulfur structure to the thermal, mechanical, and electrochemical properties of elemental-sulfur-derived polymers.

item.title: Aerogel-integrated thermal protective textiles: multidimensional performance trade-offs and adoption barriers
item.description: Aerogel-integrated thermal protective textiles have emerged as potential alternatives to conventional multilayer insulation systems, which are characterised by limited mobility, breathability and thermo-physiological comfort. This structured narrative review assesses the potential of ultralow-thermal-conductivity aerogels for wearable thermal protection. While previous reviews have addressed aerogel synthesis, fibre fabrication, mechanical reinforcement or general textile applications, and one earlier review examined the thermal, mechanical and comfort performance of aerogel clothing, this review explicitly organises the evidence around six coupled performance trade-offs and evaluates their implications for long-term service durability, manufacturing scalability and certification readiness in occupational thermal protective textiles. Coated, laminated, in situ integrated and fibre-based architectures are critically assessed. Reported thermal conductivities for selected aerogel-integrated textile systems range from approximately 0.024 W m−1 K−1 for aerogel fibre assemblies to 0.048 W m−1 K−1 for multilayer aerogel textile assemblies, although direct comparison across studies is limited by differences in textile architecture, compression state, humidity and measurement methodology. The benefits of insulation are often accompanied by decreased breathability, moisture management issues, structural fragility, or a lack of scalability. Evidence of laundering durability is highly architecture dependent; for example, one nanofibreencapsulated aerogel yarn system retained more than 97% of its initial mechanical strength after approximately 100 washing cycles under specific experimental conditions. However, laundering resistance alone does not establish long-term service durability, which additionally requires resistance to repeated flexing, abrasion, compression, perspiration and prolonged heat exposure. Additionally, existing protective-clothing standards provide relevant evaluation methods, but a dedicated framework integrating aerogel-specific degradation mechanisms and garment-level service performance remains an identified research need, and garment-level ergonomic validation is lacking. Although aerogel-integrated textiles exhibit good potential for next-generation thermal protective clothing, adoption will be determined by the balance of protection, comfort, durability and scalable manufacturing, not insulation performance alone.

item.title: Relieving Major Groove Sequestration of Poly(L-lysine) Enables Polyelectrolyte Complexation of Double-stranded RNA
item.description: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) plays a central role in gene silencing and antiviral therapeutics, yet its rigid A-form helical structure and high charge density makes it resistant to polyelectrolyte complexation compared to DNA and single-stranded RNA (ssRNA). Polyelectrolyte complex micelles (PCMs) offer a promising strategy for dsRNA delivery by leveraging electrostatic self-assembly with cationic block copolymers, but dsRNA consistently fails to form micelles under conditions where other nucleic acids assemble. Here, we show that the deep major groove of dsRNA sterically traps poly(L-lysine) (pLys), confining the polymer locally in unit complexes rather than leaving it free to bridge neighboring helices as complexation requires. Using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), transmission electron microscopy, and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we identify three factors that each shift the balance between groove-entrapped pLys and exterior-bound pLys that enables complexation, which are decreasing RNA hybridization, introducing divalent cations (Mg2+, Ca2+) that compete with major groove binding, and increasing polycation length. Each relieves entrapment through a distinct mechanism, yet all three restore the ability to form PCMs and bulk polyelectrolyte complexes with dsRNA. These findings identify major groove entrapment as the central barrier to dsRNA complexation and provide concrete design principles for engineering polyelectrolyte carriers for dsRNA-based therapeutics.

item.title: pH-dependent surface adsorption of L-tyrosine on gold surface
item.description: L-Tyrosine (L-Tyr) has been widely utilized in surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) applications to probe the structures and interactions of biomolecules on metal nanosurfaces. Nevertheless, the SERS spectral features and adsorption geometries of L-Tyr on nanosurfaces remain not fully elucidated. In this study, we report SERS spectra and adsorption geometries of L-Tyr on colloidal gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) under various pH conditions. L-Tyr adsorbs on AuNP surfaces mainly via the carboxylate group in all solution pHs (4.1­–10.6) while the deprotonated amine group also participates in the surface adsorption in neutral/basic conditions (pH = 7.5–10.6) with a pronounced adsorption geometry change to the surface. In-plane phenyl ring stretching modes, including the ν6a and aromatic ν(CH), are sensitive markers for the phenyl ring geometry upon protonation of the amine group. A molecular-level picture of the pH-dependent surface adsorption of L-Tyr on metal nanosurfaces is crucial for numerous SERS-based sensor applications, such as chiral sensing of biological molecules using L-Tyr as a reporter.

item.title: No Docking-Level pH Response of Doxorubicin Binding to a Legumin Hexamer: A Docking and pKa Survey of Candidate Release Sites
item.description: Plant storage proteins such as legumin are being studied as food-grade carriers for drugs and other bioactive molecules. A carrier for a cancer drug would have to hold its cargo at blood pH (about 7.4) and release it in acidic compartments (about pH 5 to 6). This study asked whether a legumin hexamer could do that for doxorubicin through electrostatics alone. A hexamer was predicted with AlphaFold Server (signal peptide removed) and simulated for 30 ns (GROMACS 2026.3, amber99sb-ildn, TIP3P, 310 K). Using a frame at 29.93 ns, doxorubicin was docked with AutoDock Vina at eight sites: a blinddocking groove (siteA), the protein centre, an internal void, two further fpocket pockets, and three interface sites chosen for their protonation-sensitive residues. Every site was rescored with AutoDock4 electrostatics at pH 7.4 and pH 5.0, and residue pKa values were predicted with PROPKA. The pH 5.0 receptor was built two ways: a pH-aware model that titrates only residues near the drug amine whose PROPKA pKa falls near the target range, and an over-protonated PDB2PQR/PROPKA model with 121 residues in protonated forms.

item.title: Schrödinger’s Continuous Electron Revisited: A Fourth Spatial Direction Recovers Exchange, Exclusion and the Born Rule Without Configuration Space
item.description: In 1926, Schrödinger interpreted his wave as a real, continuous distribution of electronic matter. This interpretation was soon challenged for four reasons: the many-electron wave exists in configuration space, electrons are detected as whole entities, a charged cloud would be expected to repel itself, and classical charged matter cannot possess spin or exhibit magnetism. The objective of this study is to determine the conditions under which the electron can be treated as a continuous body that addresses these objections and aligns with spectroscopic evidence, as well as to introduce a corresponding physical model of the atom. By conceptualizing the vacuum as an unbounded resonator vibrating at Ω0, electronic matter as maintaining this resonance, and the nucleus as a compact 1/r source, the vacuum-resonance continuous-matter (VRCM) model provides a physical foundation for the atom. This model further conceptualizes the electron as a continuous body extending into a real fourth spatial direction (w), with a maximum extent of 2.6 × 10–19 m, and whose portions are defined by pattern, fold, and side. A single calibrated action unit, , reproduced fifteen lines of H, He+, and Li2+ within 2.9 ppm, and one value of Γ fitted five measured hydrogen transitions within 1.3 × 10–9. Unlike non-relativistic quantum mechanics, which postulates the sign reversal upon exchanging two electrons, VRCM derives it from the geometry of its body, which is non-orientable and returns only after 720°. With each place holding one hydrogen-equivalent of matter and a face rule taken as a premise, each pattern accommodates only two portions, one on each side, which accounted for the shells from hydrogen to neon, lithium’s 2s below its 2p within 3%, the ground terms from boron to fluorine through Hund’s first two rules, and the triplet ground state of O2. The diamagnetism of helium and the paramagnetic susceptibility of O2 agreed within 0.7% and 0.5%, respectively, and the ionization energy of lithium came out at 5.409 eV against the measured 5.392 eV. Helium’s two portions share one three-dimensional region and are separated only along w; without w, its energy rises by at least 20 eV. A coupling of the vibrations of the two portions through w, fixed on helium alone, brought the correlation energies of the helium-like ions from Li+ to Ne+8 within 0.1% and of H– within 1.6%. Within one side, the self-repulsion of the body is cancelled exactly by exchange, while portions on opposite sides repel with full strength. With the coupling between the two faces taken as a premise, a two-face law gave g = 2, the two kinds of charge as the two faces, and Dirac’s small component as matter spilled onto the second face. The vacuum’s zero-point vibrations gave the Lamb shift of hydrogen as 1050.74 MHz at one loop, against the measured 1057.8 MHz, and the electron’s anomalous magnetic moment as α/2. Aside from spectra, the same body accounted for its detection as a whole: its wavelength followed from the vacuum’s wave rule, and the Born odds from the body remaining whole as it contracts onto one place at capture, given a detection threshold taken as a premise. Each premise in this model was adopted only after its alternative failed by a stated margin. These results suggest that continuous electronic matter connected through the fourth spatial direction (w) can recover the exchange sign, exclusion and the Born rule without configuration space, while accounting for spin, magnetism and the absence of selfrepulsion.

item.title: Programmed switching gives multiblock copolymers of uniform composition
Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Novel Acetamides as Selective MAO-B Inhibitors against Parkinson’s Disease: Alleviating Oxidative Stress and Mitochondrial Dysfunction
item.description: We have synthesized a diverse set of acetamides and tested their activity against Monoamine Oxidase (MAO) enzymes. MAO-A and MAO-B activities were measured using the MAO-Glo bioluminescent assay, and the MTT assay assessed the cytotoxicity of the molecules. Most of the molecules showed cell viability >87% at the high dose of 10.0 µM. Cytotoxicity of <10% was observed for RA3 and RA6, compared with the other molecules, and cell viability was >95%. Further, these molecules were assessed for their neuroprotective potential in an in vitro MPP+-induced PD model in BE (2)-M17 cells. Compounds RA3 and RA6 reversed MPP+induced cell death, with RA3 showing a significant increase in cell viability (83.23%) compared with MPP+-treated cells (58%). Moreover, RA6 showed a significantly greater inhibitory effect on MAO-B than on MAO-A, substantiating its selectivity for MAO-B, with an IC50 of 4.67±0.02 and a Ki of 2.33±0.01. The study on ROS and Ca2+ indicates that the molecule RA-6 reduces intracellular ROS production and calcium influx by mitigating MPP+induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial damage. Its binding affinity reveals pi-alkyl and hydrogen bonds with amino residues near the FAD cofactor, such as Tyr326 and Tyr398, and with Tyr398 and Tyr435, which are well-established components of the MAO-B substrate cavity. This excitotoxicity plays a major role in neurodegeneration, and RA6 is indicated to have dual MAO-B inhibition and ion channel modulation, making it a promising neuroprotective lead.

item.title: Ruthenium-Catalysed Hydrogenative Depolymerisation of Polyimides to a Tetraol and it’s Application in Alkyd Resin Synthesis
item.description: The chemical recycling of high-performance polyimides remains challenging owing to their exceptional chemical and thermal stability. Herein, we report a tandem aminolysis–hydrogenation strategy for the depolymerisation and valorisation of Kapton waste, affording 4,4′-oxydianiline (ODA) and benzene-1,2,4,5tetrayltetramethanol (tetraol). The process combines ethanolamine-mediated aminolysis with catalytic hydrogenation using a Ru-MACHO-BH pincer complex under 30 bar of H2 at 150 °C. The method was demonstrated on real-world Kapton-containing waste, including adhesive-backed tape and a heater, enabling the recovery of valuable organic products. To demonstrate its potential for materials upcycling, the tetraol was used as an alternative to pentaerythritol in the synthesis of alkyd resins from soybean and olive oils. The resulting resins exhibited thermal stability and rheological behaviour dependent on the polyol and oil employed, with the soybean oil-based tetraol resin showing higher viscosity and sag resistance. This work establishes a route from polyimide waste to a functional polyol and demonstrates its potential as a building block for alkyd resin synthesis.

item.title: Identifying SABRE-Active Iridium Complexes with Carboxylate Ligands through Relativistic DFT-NMR
item.description: Correlation of computed chemical shifts with experimental NMR resonances provides a valuable tool for assigning SABRE-active dihydride complexes in solution. However, dealing with iridium-based complexes requires consideration of heavy-atom relativistic spin–orbit effects. In this work, an extensive 34-complex benchmark consolidates a zero-order regular approximation (ZORA) spin–orbit density functional theory (DFT) protocol for chemical shift prediction of hydrides. Specifically, this computational framework resolves coordination ambiguities in several SABRE-active intermediates here experimentally investigated, confirming a preference for monodentate carboxylate binding in pyruvate, oxalate, and formate ligands. Furthermore, incorporating calculated scalar J-coupling constants into spin dynamics simulations allows the calculation of the polarization profile as a function of the magnetic field for formate-bound species. Also in this case, the theoretical predictions are supported by the observation of 1H SABRE polarization of formate under the adopted experimental conditions.

item.title: Does a non-Newtonian regime exist in polymer brush bilayers under steady-state shear?
item.description: In this article, I address the question of whether a non-Newtonian regime exists in polymer brush bilayers under steady-state shear. For this, I use molecular dynamics simulations with a DPD thermostat that takes hydrodynamic interactions into account. The solvent is treated explicitly to capture the most significant hydrodynamic effects. My simulations over the Weissenberg number range from 0.9 to 3.5 show no sign of a non-Newtonian regime and the shear stress remains linear with respect to the Weissenberg number. The simulation of a charged system with a Bjerrum length of 0.7, which is that of water, shows no non-Newtonian regime and its prefactor is larger. The larger prefactor of the charged system appears to be due to both step-like density profile of the brush as well as the formation of counterion clusters in the interpenetration zone. The normal stress does not change over the range studied. The results of this research are a step forward in our understanding of this complex soft matter system and they reveal how friction works in biological environments such as the mammalian knee joint.

item.title: Near Autonomous Discovery of One-pot Carbon-Carbon Bond Formation through Reductive Amination and DPPH-mediated Nitrogen Deletion
item.description: Primary amines and aldehydes are widely available building blocks whose carbon frameworks can be joined through secondary amine formation followed by nitrogen deletion. Here we combine reductive amination with O-(diphenylphosphinyl)hydroxylamine (DPPH)-mediated nitrogen deletion and establish a one-pot implementation without intermediate solvent evaporation, work-up or purification. The initial hypothesis and baseline protocol were proposed near-autonomously using Gemini and Maria; chemists performed the initial validation and co-designed the subsequent high-throughput campaign. Across 1,728 two-stage microscale experiments comparing reductive amination and N-alkylation routes, screening identified productive substrate-condition combinations and supported further development of the reductive amination sequence. Bench-scale evaluation of nine amine-aldehyde pairs demonstrated that selected products could be isolated using a concentrated one-pot protocol, although overall yields remained modest and performance depended strongly on substrate identity. Together, these results extend DPPH-mediated nitrogen deletion to a reductive-amination workflow and demonstrate a practical one-pot sequence, providing a complementary disconnection for accessing carbon-linked products from common amine and aldehyde building blocks.

item.title: Chirality-Dependent Packing and the Visible LMCT Band of Arylethynyl-Substituted Ru(β-diketonate)3 Complexes: A Computational Study
item.description: Tris(β-diketonato)ruthenium(III) complexes with arylethynyl arms (Ru-Cn) absorb at about 665 nm in solution and in enantiopure thin films but at 733 nm in racemic films. We examine the origin of this chirality dependence computationally for the three model complexes Ru-H, Ru-OMe, and Ru-C1, which have phenylethynyl, 4-methoxyphenylethynyl, and 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylethynyl arms, respectively, with dispersion-corrected DFT, TD-DFT, and a transition-charge exciton model applied to dimers, chains, and the racemic crystal. For Ru-OMe, homochiral and heterochiral pairs form face-to-face dimers of similar geometry, the homochiral one being 5 kcal mol−1 more stable, and the exciton coupling V is small (|V| ≤ 160 cm−1) in every arrangement, so aggregation shifts the band by less than 10 nm; this result holds with a triple-ζ basis set and with the range-separated functional ωB97X-D3, and Ru-C1 behaves in the same way (homochiral preference 5.2 kcal mol−1, |V| ≤ 101 cm−1). The molecular geometry matters far more, and the geometric parameters differ in the direction of their effect. For Ru-OMe, rotating the aryl rings from the perpendicular orientation into the chelate plane shifts the band to the red (559 → 690 nm), so that the planar conformation reproduces the solution band, and elongating the Ru–O bonds shifts it further to the red (13 nm per 0.01 Å). For both Ru-OMe and Ru-C1, an arm forced to within 4 Å of a neighboring Ru(III) center admixes intermolecular charge transfer and shifts the band to the red as well; the admixture is 20–40% with PBE0, which overestimates it, and at most 16% with ωB97X-D3, and such a contact is not an energy minimum of an isolated pair. The 780–800-nm bands obtained for the arm-over-metal dimers at semiempirical geometries arise mainly from the elongated Ru–O bonds of those geometries. A thin film of racemic Ru-H, measured here, absorbs at 650 nm, 12 nm to the red of its solution band (638 nm), so the parent compound shows no racemate-specific shift and the 733-nm band requires the alkoxy groups. The band of the racemic condensed state is therefore attributed to packing-imposed changes in molecular geometry (Ru–O distances, alkoxy torsion, or an enforced intermolecular contact), not to exciton (J-aggregate) coupling.

item.title: ChemomHarness: An Extensible Research Infrastructure for Human-in-the-Loop Spectroscopic Modeling
item.description: Spectroscopic modeling is an iterative process in which researchers continually evaluate and refine workflows centered on analytical objectives. Validation results guide choices of preprocessing, spectral range, and model complexity, yet final models and error metrics reveal little about how alternatives were compared or chosen. While large language model (LLM) agents offer a natural-language interface for coordinating multistep analyses, single automated runs lack ongoing researcher oversight and redirection, runtime verification of validation boundaries, and crosssession continuity. To address these limitations, we present ChemomHarness, a research infrastructure for human-in-the-loop spectroscopic research with three principal contributions. First, researchers interact with an agent through a workbench to review evidence after each computation, steer modeling directions, and branch from any historical point as evidence accumulates. Second, a runtime harness enforces programmatic scientific rules prior to model fitting to verify sample 2 independence and allowable estimation scopes, blocking out-of-bounds operations without relying on prompt compliance. Third, exploration and model dossiers separately preserve structured investigation histories and individual model artifacts, enabling incoming agents to resume studies and reconstruct existing models. Additionally, ChemomHarness provides a plug-in interface and standalone inference package exports. Benchmarked with near-infrared partial least squares regression (PLSR), the infrastructure reliably enforces scientific rules, reproduces numerical outputs across agents, sustains research handoffs, and supports algorithm extension and model deployment.

item.title: Inhibiting LINE-1 retrotransposons therapeutically in disease
item.description: The LINE-1 retrotransposon is a virus-like genomic element that can activate in diseased cells. It has been implicated in cancer, autoimmunity, developmental disorders, infectious disease and neurodegeneration. LINE-1 can be inhibited by reverse transcriptase inhibitors, small molecules originally developed for HIV. The correlation between HIV and LINE-1 inhibition is 0.89 on a log scale, in spite of >450 Mya of evolutionary history since retroviruses diverged from retrotransposons. Suppression of HIV requires prevention of a completed 9.7 kb virus insertion into the genome in immune cells. However, every cell in the body already contains >100 copies of LINE-1 that can potentially activate. Even incomplete LINE-1 mediated insertions can cause damaging mutations and genome instability. Furthermore, partial HIV and LINE-1 products in the cytoplasm of cells can contribute to an inflammatory immune response. Preclinical studies have shown LINE-1 inhibitors slow the progression of otherwise unrelated diseases. LINE-1’s contribution to these diseases can potentially be quantified using single-nucleus whole-genome sequencing on diseased tissue, enabling prioritization of disease selection for therapeutic development. Furthermore, LINE-1’s ORF1p protein can be measured in the blood of individuals with certain cancers. LINE-1 inhibitors could therefore be extended to various diseases. Potentially used both as an anti-inflammatory and prophylactically to help preserve genome integrity. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are available at low cost for HIV, and higher doses of some could be used to inhibit LINE-1. However, reverse transcriptase inhibitors do not prevent DNA cutting by LINE-1’s endonuclease. Novel inhibitors may therefore be required. This, combined with novel diagnostics opens up possibilities for inhibiting LINE-1 therapeutically in disease

item.title: MOF-Confined Pt-V₉O₂₈ Interfacial Clusters as a Model Platform for Probing C-H Bond Activation in Hydrocarbon Oxidation
item.description: Light hydrocarbon oxidation is fundamentally limited by the inertness of C-H bonds and the structural complexity of heterogeneous catalysts, which obscures the identification of genuine active sites. Here, we report atomically precise PtV9O28 clusters confined within the Zr-based metal-organic framework NU1K, establishing a structurally well-defined platform of isolated Pt-V interfacial sites. This system serves as a model platform that enables direct correlation between atomic structure and catalytic function. Combined spectroscopic and kinetic analyses reveal that these interfacial sites lower the barrier for C-H bond activation, likely through cooperative interactions between cationic Pt centers and neighboring vanadium-oxo species. Kinetic measurements show that the apparent activation energy for propane oxidation is substantially reduced relative to oxide-supported analogues, consistent with facilitated C-H bond scission at the interface. Beyond catalytic performance, this work establishes atomically defined interfacial clusters as a model system to unambiguously identify active sites and probe interfacial C-H activation in heterogeneous catalysis.

item.title: A unified perspective on AI for secure, safe, and sustainable molecules and materials discovery
item.description: Safety, security, and sustainability (S3) - encompassing risks to human health, ecosystems, and societal impacts are crucial dimensions in molecular and materials design. Parallelly, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific discovery, offering new avenues to tackle complex chemical design challenges. Yet, systematically integration of S3 objectives into AIdriven chemical discovery remains underexplored. Through an AI-assisted network analysis of 8,417 studies - spanning drug, polymers, organic electronics, batteries, semiconductors, catalysts, and thermoelectric discoveries - we find current efforts are dominated by property and function prediction, while only 7.1% explicitly incorporate S3-related considerations. To bridge this gap, we provide a structured overview of S3 metrics and their potential applications in AI-guided molecular and materials discovery. We then identify relevant data infrastructures, and highlight how S3 metrics can be integrated into design workflows through state-of-the-art multitask models, active learning, and generative AI. We outline recommendations for interoperable data sharing and robust benchmarks across chemistry and materials communities, and finally highlight key challenges including model interpretability and uncertainty in low-data settings, multi-objective trade-offs, synthesizability, and the misuse potential of chemical AI. Our framework supports the integration of S3 metrics into AI-guided design workflows, redefining the foundations for the next generation molecular and materials discovery.

item.title: Phosphonium–Catechol-Coated Oxide Nanoparticles as Dispersing Units for Boron Nitride in Poly(amic acid) and Polyimide Films
item.description: The aggregation of inorganic fillers in polymer composites hinders uniform dispersion and limits mechanicalreinforcement.Inthisstudy,weemployAl2O3andantimony-dopedtinoxide nanoparticlescoatedwithtributyl[2-(N-(3,4-dihydroxyphenethyl)carbamoyl)ethyl]phosphonium chloride (TPC),alow-molecular-weightdispersantbearing catecholgroups and phosphonium cations, as dispersing units for hexagonal boron nitride (BN) particles. Following bead-millingassisted hybridization, the BN dispersions exhibited number-weighted DLS distributions centered near 400 nm and remained stable in methanol. SEM and XPS observations supported island-like attachment of the nanoparticles to BN surfaces. Moreover, the hybrid particles retained positive zeta potentials. The improved dispersion was maintained in poly(amic acid) (PAA) cast films. The spectral haze at 2500 nm decreased from 95.5% for the BN-only film to 16.6% at a nominal 30 wt % BN@T-Al2O3 loading. The Young’s modulus and maximum stress increased by 47.0% and 38.8%,respectively,relativetoBN-only,andcomparablethermaldiffusivityandelectrical insulation were retained. The improved BN dispersion was retained after thermal imidization at 300 °C, and the relative degree of imidization reached 95.0%. These results demonstrate that TPC-coated nanoparticles can suppress BN aggregation without direct chemical modification of BN and improve the mechanical performance and processability of polymer composite films. The use of inorganic nanoparticles as dispersants can serve as a novel materials-design strategy for controlling filler dispersion and composite properties.

item.title: An Automated Multi-Material Powder Dosing, Blending, and Formulation Evaluation Platform
item.description: Early-stage formulation development requires the preparation and analysis of many candidate powder blends from limited quantities of material, a task that remains slow, manual, and difficult to automate for solids. This work presents an automated platform that integrates multi-material powder dosing, pneumatic blending, automated cleaning, and robotic-assisted analytical assessment within a single coordinated workflow, enabling autonomous preparation and evaluation of gram-scale blends. Vacuum-assisted volumetric dosing achieved a linear volume-to-mass response for all nine materials tested (R2 ≥ 0.99), with mean relative dosing errors within ±2.5% for seven out of nine raw materials and relative standard deviations typically below 1% for fillers and 1.1 – 2.5% for the model active ingredient paracetamol. Across 173 binary and ternary blends, within-blend spectral dispersion measured by near-infrared spectroscopy indicated consistent spectral homogeneity, with five blends flagged as atypical. Under integrated dosing and blending, NIR prediction of paracetamol content agreed with nominal targets within the prediction uncertainty of the model between 10 and 30 wt. %, with within-blend relative standard deviations of 2.0–3.7% between 15 and 30 wt. % meeting the 5% blend-uniformity criterion. Fully autonomous sequential preparation of 12 formulations was completed in approximately six hours without manual intervention, with between-replicate reproducibility below 5% relative standard deviation. Systematic between-formulation carryover, increasing with drug loading, identified automated cleaning efficiency as the principal limitation of the current system and the primary target for further development. The platform provides a material-efficient, analytically integrated route to autonomous formulation development.

item.title: Fragility in hybrid glass formers: Structural dimensionality and rheology–calorimetry correlations
item.description: We correlate the fragility index of various hybrid inorganicorganic glass formers using rheological and calorimetric techniques, demonstrating that both methods are valid when technical limitations allow for only one. Structural dimensionality influences the fragility index, with lowerdimensional hybrid glass formers exhibiting fragile behaviour, whilst three-dimensional hybrid glass formers display intermediate fragility.

item.title: AI Agents for Biochemical Discovery: From Open-Ended Hypotheses to Closed-Loop Evidence
item.description: Language-model agents can retrieve evidence, formulate mechanisms, propose molecular interventions, and coordinate computational analyses, while self-driving laboratories can select, execute, and evaluate experiments over many rounds. These advances are often presented as parts of a single progression towards autonomous discovery. The evidence instead reveals two partially disconnected frontiers. Open-ended systems operate over broad scientific questions but still rely on researchers to turn their proposals into discriminating and executable experiments. Systems with strong physical closure act with less supervision, but generally do so after the hypothesis space, available actions, measurement pipeline, and success criterion have been specified. We argue that the missing capability is hypothesis–experiment co-design: constructing a hypothesis together with a test that can discriminate among alternatives, compiling that test into an executable protocol, preserving the provenance of the resulting observation, and revising the hypothesis from the evidence. We decompose this capability into five auditable interfaces and use them to distinguish stage coverage from interface authorship, operational from epistemic closure, terminal validation from in-loop evidence, and claimed from demonstrated autonomy. This view reorganizes current work in molecular design, computational evaluation, laboratory execution, and scientific agents around the evidence that actually closes their loops. It also exposes a common limit on self-evolving agents: in biochemistry, improving a research strategy requires a verification signal that is often physical, slow, and expensive. The near-term path is therefore not checkpoint-free autonomy, but selective autonomy across interfaces that can be represented, checked, and audited.

item.title: Probing the molecular determinants of Des1 inhibition through structure-guided modification of the N-acyl region of PR280
item.description: Dihydroceramide desaturase 1 (Des1) has emerged as an attractive therapeutic target for the modulation of sphingolipid metabolism. In our previous work, the cyclopropenone-containing ceramide analogue PR280 was identified as a potent Des1 inhibitor. Analysis of a holo Fe₂O₂-Des1 structural model suggested that the N-acyl region of the inhibitor occupied a relatively permissive binding pocket and therefore offered promising opportunities for further optimization. To investigate the contribution of this region to Des1 recognition, a virtual library comprising 2027 analogues was generated and evaluated using a structure-guided workflow. Eight representative compounds bearing structurally diverse N-acyl substituents were synthesized through an efficient deprotection–amidation sequence employing a stable aminodiol hydrochloride intermediate and HATU-mediated coupling. While computational studies predicted improved protein-ligand interactions for several analogues, biological evaluation revealed that modification of the N-acyl region failed to improve activity relative to PR280. Analysis of in situ and in vitro DES1 activity revealed that many of the analogues had almost completely lost their inhibitory effects on DES1 compared to parental PR280, with PR280-8 showing inhibition but at a lower degree than PR280. Detailed analysis of the computational and biological data suggests that factors not fully captured by conventional docking approaches, including conformational effects, desolvation penalties, and local protein-ligand interactions, play a critical role in determining Des1 inhibition. These findings highlight the challenges of structure-based optimization within the amphiphilic Des1 binding cavity and provide new insights into the molecular determinants governing ligand recognition by this enzyme.

item.title: Electropolymerized Fe(II) Polypyridyl Films on ZnO Nanowire Photoelectrodes: Electrochemical Response, Photopotential, and Photocurrent Characterization
item.description: Redox-active molecular films can modify semiconductor interfaces, yet the influence of nanostructuring on charge transfer in these hybrid systems remains poorly understood. Here, two Fe(II) polypyridyl films were electropolymerized on ZnO nanowire (ZnOnw) photoelectrodes using distinct routes based on amine oxidation and diazonium reduction. Both films exhibited similar non-ideal electrochemical behavior on ZnOnw, characterized by high peak-to-peak separations during electropolymerization, peak currents with a scan-rate dependence typical of diffusion-controlled systems, and the appearance of an additional reduction process. These features suggest that the nanostructured architecture may affect charge propagation within the composite electrode. The influence of the polymer overlayer on the physical and photoelectrochemical characterization of ZnO was also investigated. While the optical band-gap remained unchanged, Mott-Schottky analysis appeared unreliable for nanostructured ZnO. In contrast, a galvanostatic photopotential approach provided a more reliable alternative for estimating the band edge on bare semiconductors: the zero-current intercept of 2.54 V vs Li+/Li was consistent with the expected conduction-band edge of planar ZnO (≈ 2.6 V vs Li+/Li), suggesting its possible utilization for estimating the band edge of bare nanostructured electrodes. Photocurrent measurements and electrochromism under illumination further complemented the assessment of the photoelectrochemical response of the hybrid electrodes. Overall, this work describes how electrode nanostructuring influences the electrochemical response of Fe(II) polypyridyl films, whereas the polymer overlayer affects the photoelectrochemical characterization of ZnO and enables electronic communication between the two components under illumination. The differences between the two polymerization platforms were comparatively minor, suggesting that the amount of deposited material plays a more significant role than the polymerization route in determining the overall electrochemical response.

item.title: Automated error assessment for density functional theory calculations of hydrocarbons
item.description: * Correspondence to: mattia.salomone@ehu.es, jingshan.luo@nankai.edu.cn, federico.calle@ehu.es Abstract Reliable gas-phase hydrocarbon thermochemistry is necessary for the modelling of countless processes of industrial, technological and environmental importance. Currently, there are sizable errors in the formation enthalpies of hydrocarbons calculated with density functional theory that increase alongside the size and complexity of molecules. Here we provide three error correction schemes and apply them to a fitting set and a test set. The formation enthalpies in the fitting set calculated with seven exchange-correlation functionals are reproduced with nearly chemical accuracy on the basis of the number of 2 C atoms, and by decomposing molecular errors into additive contributions by bonds or groups of atoms. The latter two correction schemes are transferable to the more complex hydrocarbons in the test set and yield accurate hydrogenation and C–C coupling enthalpies. Cross-functional analysis further illustrates the systematicity of DFT-based errors and the connections between functionals.

item.title: Bimolecular 1,3-Difunctionalization of m-Arynes with Ethynylbenziodoxoles
item.description: meta-Benzyne (m-benzyne) is a highly reactive intermediate with unique electronic properties, yet its intermolecular difunctionalization remains challenging due to spatially separated 1,3reactive sites. Herein, we report a bimolecular 1,3-difunctionalization of m-arynes employing ethynylbenziodoxoles (EBXs). The reaction proceeds under fluoride-mediated conditions and enables the simultaneous introduction of alkynyl and λ3-iodanyl groups across the m-benzyne framework, providing access to a variety of 1-alkynyl-3iodanyl arenes. A range of substituted m-benzyne precursors and EBX reagents are compatible with the transformation, furnishing the corresponding products in moderate to good yields. Mechanistic experiments revealed that distinct precursor isomers converge to identical product distributions, supporting the intermediacy of common m-benzyne species. Furthermore, crossover experiments employing two distinct EBX reagents showed no detectable crossover products, indicating that alkynyl and iodanyl fragments are transferred as a pair from the same EBX molecule. This work expands the synthetic chemistry of m-benzyne beyond simple nucleophilic trapping, demonstrating that this long-elusive aryne can engage in controlled bimolecular 1,3-difunctionalization.

item.title: CP2Ksol: A Poisson–Boltzmann Implicit Electrolyte for Constant-Potential and Hybrid-Solvent Simulations in CP2K
item.description: First-principles simulations of electrified metal/water interfaces need an electrolyte model that describes the charging and polarization of the electrode, a hybrid solvent that joins explicit water to a continuum, and control of the electrode potential. item.title: Differentiable Coarse-Graining of Phase Equilibria: Learning a Crystallizable Water Model
item.description: Bottom-up coarse-grained (CG) models are derived from the configurations of a reference model, either by approximating its many-body potential of mean force or by matching its structural correlations, but neither route ensures that the phase equilibria of the reference are reproduced. Trained with differentiable coarse-graining (DiffCG) on the mapped structure and pressure of ice Ih and liquid TIP4P/Ice water, a onebead many-body neural-network model reproduces the densities and radial distribution functions of both phases but predicts a melting temperature 62.5K below that of the reference. We extend DiffCG to phase equilibria by refining this model with an additional objective, the ice–liquid chemical-potential difference at the reference melting temperature, while its structural and pressure objectives are retained. The free-energy anchor is taken from the CG model’s own coexistence point by Gibbs–Helmholtz integration, so that no absolute free energies are required, and changes of the phase free energies are tracked by fixed-cell reweighting with Bennett acceptance ratio offsets.

item.title: Hierarchical symmetry breaking in bilateral paper wasp forewings: vibrational circular dichroism reveals hidden chirality upon folding
item.description: Biological materials often derive their functions from hierarchical organization beyond the molecular scale. Although chirality is conventionally associated with molecular stereochemistry, chiroptical responses can also emerge from symmetry breaking at higher levels of organization. Whether such hierarchical handedness emerges dynamically in functional biological structures remains largely unexplored. Here, we use microscopic vibrational circular dichroism (MultiDVCD) imaging to map the protein–chitin architecture of paper wasp forewings with a spatial resolution of 100 μm. In the fully extended state, anatomically corresponding regions of the left and right forewings exhibited nearly identical VCD spectra in the amide I and II regions, consistent with similar protein secondary structures. Folding, however, unveiled a hidden bilateral chiroptical asymmetry: the paired wings developed opposite VCD responses, with a pronounced sign reversal in the left wing. Electromagnetic simulations showed that reversing the relative twist between anisotropic layers was sufficient to reverse the circular-polarization-dependent response without altering the underlying molecular properties. These results support a model in which folding transforms intrinsically similar molecular organizations into opposite, mirror-related mesoscale chiroptical states. Our findings reveal how mechanical transformation of a biological structure can 3 reorganize molecular anisotropy to generate emergent optical handedness, establishing vibrational chiroptical imaging as a powerful probe of hierarchical organization in biological materials.

item.title: Self-assembly of monovalent anion pillared metal-organic frameworks: linker functionalization matters
item.description: Monovalent anion pillaring in coordination networks remains a challenging design target because charge balance requires the simultaneous incorporation of additional counteranions within the structure. Here, we show that subtle changes in the substitution pattern of bis(imidazolyl)benzene (bib) linkers can strongly alter the outcome of self-assembly in Cu(II)-based systems with monovalent polyatomic anions. The dimethoxy-substituted ligand 1,1'-(2,5-dimethoxy-1,4-phenylene)bis(1H-imidazole) (bib(OMe)2) reacts with Cu(BF4)2, Cu(ClO4)2 and Cu(NO3)2 to afford three isoreticular monovalent anion-pillared frameworks, {Cu[bib(OMe)2]2X}X (X = BF4−, UdP-30; ClO4−, UdP-31; NO3−, UdP-32), in which Cu-bib(OMe)2 layers are connected by coordinated anions while additional charge-balancing anions are located within the pores. The frameworks crystallize in the monoclinic C2/c space group and differ from previously reported bibCF3-based topological analogues (UdP-10, -11, and -12, containing the same anions) in symmetry, layer geometry, anion arrangement, and pore accessibility. These compounds retain crystallinity upon desolvation and possess accessible microporosity, as evidenced by gas sorption analysis.

item.title: AGROS: An Integrated Multimodal AI Framework for Autonomous Navigation, Robotic Manipulation, and Intelligent Task Automation
item.description: The latest advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Distributed Computing have opened new potential for intelligent robotic assistants capable of executing self-managed tasks and enabling intelligent human-robot interaction (HRI). In this paper, the authors present the Automated Guided Robotic Operating System (AGROS), a multimodal autonomous robotic system that integrates intelligent task automation, cognitive reasoning, vision, and autonomous navigation (Nav2), enabling task automation in residential environments. The proposed architecture comprises a distributed communication system built on the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) middleware layer and Raspberry Pi 5 and ESP32 microcontrollers. It includes object detection (YOLOv8), visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), Real-Time Appearance-Based Mapping (RTAB-Map), Nav2, inverse-kinematics-based manipulation (MoveIt 2), and multimodal, context-aware interaction with OpenAI Whisper, Google Gemini Vision-Language Model (VLM), and Piper text-to-speech (TTS). The experimental results demonstrate that confidence scores for object categorization can range from 0.91 to 0.97 across three real-world test scenarios. This multimodal communication pipeline is handled in an average of 2.8 s: 500 ms for voice recognition, 1900 ms for multimodal reasoning, and 400 ms for speech synthesis. Localization drift has been reduced to 1.5 cm at a trip distance of 5 m, which is 83.3% of the overall 9.0 cm localization drift. The navigation framework can successfully generate a 0.82 m-long collisionfree path in a congested region. Furthermore, the robotic manipulator can achieve pick-andplace success rates of 82%, 94%, and 76% for small, medium, and large objects, respectively. The examination of computational resources shows that visual SLAM, motion planning, ROS 2-based navigation, and VLM communication consume 45%, 25%, 20%, and 10% of the compute node’s CPU resources, respectively. The results reveal that the combination of multimodal AI and distributed robotic control can be used to build a scalable, resourceefficient, and context-aware robotic assistant that autonomously performs daily tasks and supports smart living systems.

item.title: Atom-centre and shell dependent correlation factors in F12 theory
item.description: We propose an extension of the fixed-amplitude ansatz in F12 theory using Slater-type correlation factors, allowing for the assignment of different range parameters γ to specific atoms or atomic subshells. The central idea of this extension is to make the correlation factor dependent on atomic basis function shells. We demonstrate that the established approximations of F12 theory can be transferred to this new approach. Numerical examples from our pilot implementation confirm improvements in two scenarios: systems containing atoms that require strongly different range parameters, and the balanced description of valence and core-valence correlation effects. The proposed approach remains orbital invariant and does not require the optimisation of additional coefficients. By removing the requirement for a single range parameter, it enables the development of size-consistent model chemistries with locally optimal correlation factors.

item.title: Electrophotochemical Dehydrogenative Cyclization of N-Allyl Ureas to Exocyclic Methylene-Containing Cyclic Isoureas
item.description: Exocyclic alkylidene cyclic isoureas are valuable heterocycles, yet their synthesis relies on alkyne precursors and precious-metal catalysts. Herein we report an electrophotochemical dehydrogenative cyclization of readily available N-allyl ureas to 5-methylene oxazolidin-2-imines, merging Rose Bengal photocatalysis with anodic oxidation. The reaction proceeds under constant current (15 mA) with visible-light irradiation, without metals or chemical oxidants, and releases H2 as the sole by-product. The scope of twenty-two substrates was shown, with up to 71% yield and exclusive retention of the exocyclic olefin. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction follows a radical pathway. Anodic oxidation and subsequent photoexcitation of the Rose Bengal photocatalyst generate a strongly oxidizing excited state, which is crucial to the success of the protocol. This excited state undergoes single-electron transfer (SET) with the substrate, forming an N-centered radical intermediate. Dehydrogenative cyclization of this intermediate then yields the desired product.

item.title: Automated Corner Detection for Shape Characterization of Molecular Cages
item.description: Porous molecular cages pack into solid-state materials whose void structure depends on the macro-scale shape of the molecule itself, yet existing computational tools characterize what is inside a cage—its windows, cavity, or host-guest fit—rather than the cage’s overall shape, and reference-free descriptors that generalize across topologically distinct cages remain largely undeveloped. We introduce a fully automated, reference-free pipeline that detects a cage’s corners directly from its atomic coordinates: a minimum-error ellipsoid fit distinguishes corner atoms from those belonging to the molecular skeleton; later, a persistence-based score quantifies how robustly each atom is classified under controlled inflation of the fitted ellipsoid, and a two-stage clustering process groups together atoms into corner clusters, allowing for automated corner count and characterization. Against a manually annotated validation set of 53 knowntopology structures, this advanced-clustering pipeline achieves a 88.7% 1-off accuracy on classification, with an exact corner-count accuracy of 69.8%. Applied to a repository of 8,909 porous cage-like structures mined from the Crystallography Open Database, the resulting shape descriptors—corner count, elongation, corner composition and homogeneity, and internal/external protrusion distances—show internally consistent, mechanistically explicable correlations among themselves and are largely orthogonal to established porosity descriptors, supporting their use as a genuine complement to, rather than a substitute for, existing porosity characterization.

item.title: An aqueous all-iron redox flow battery based on a cluster compound
item.description: The development of near-neutral all-soluble all-iron redox flow batteries relies on negative-electrolyte active species with suitable redox potentials and good electrochemical reversibility. Existing research has focused primarily on tailoring the coordination environments of mononuclear iron complexes. Here, we introduce the sodium salt of a nitrosyl iron–sulfur cluster (Na[Fe4S3(NO)7]·5H2O) as an active species for aqueous negolytes. Featuring a distinct multinuclear Fe–S–NO coordination framework, the cluster exhibits an apparent redox midpoint potential of −0.684 V versus the saturated calomel electrode and apparent diffusion coefficients of approximately 1.0×10-5 cm2 s-1 in an aqueous electrolyte, retaining a relatively stable redox response over 500 cyclic voltammetry scans. Natural bond orbital analysis indicates that one-electron reduction involves electron redistribution across multiple iron centers and their associated coordination units, revealing a multicenter electronic response distinct from that of mononuclear iron complexes. Pairing the cluster with sodium ferrocyanide yields a near-neutral all-soluble all-iron redox flow battery with an apparent redox potential difference of approximately 0.90 V. The battery completes 176 charge–discharge cycles at 1 mA cm-2, maintaining Coulombic and energy efficiencies of approximately 99% and 85%, respectively, with a capacity retention of approximately 80%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of multinuclear nitrosyl iron–sulfur clusters as redox-active species for flow batteries, broaden the design space for all-iron negolytes beyond mononuclear iron complexes, and provide an experimental and theoretical basis for developing aqueous energy storage materials with multicenter redox characteristics.

item.title: Mitochondrial G-Quadruplex-Binding Ruthenium(II) Complexes Remodel Cancer Cell Respiration and mtDNA-Encoded Gene Expression
item.description: Mitochondrial DNA G-quadruplexes (G4s) represent emerging yet largely unexplored targets for anticancer therapy. Herein, we report two triphenylphosphonium (TPP)-functionalized Ru(II) polypyridyl complexes (1 and 2) designed to combine mitochondrial targeting with G4 recognition. Spectroscopic investigations revealed strong interactions with mitochondrial G4s, although these were partially attenuated by competing duplex DNA. Both complexes exhibited cytostatic activity against HCT116 colorectal cancer cells in 2D and 3D models, accompanied by concentration- and time-dependent cellular accumulation. Notably, their activity was synergistically enforced by combination with metformin or the glucose transporter inhibitor BAY-876. Seahorse metabolic profiling revealed substantial perturbations of cellular bioenergetics, affecting mitochondrial respiration, extracellular acidification, and ATP production. Most strikingly, quantitative real-time PCR revealed a marked and selective downregulation of mitochondrially encoded genes, while nuclear gene expression remained widely unaffected. Together, these findings identify mitochondria-targeted Ru(II) complexes 1 and 2 as promising modulators of mitochondrial gene expression and energy metabolism, highlighting a potential strategy for anticancer intervention.

item.title: Pulse Electrodeposition of Gold in a Deep Eutectic Solvent: Effects of Cathodic Potential and Pulse Asymmetry on Particle Morphology
item.description: This study reports the electrodeposition of faceted gold nanostructures with concave morphologies in a choline chloride–urea deep eutectic solvent (DES) using potential pulses. The applied potential pulses alternated between a cathodic potential selected from -0.20 V to -0.45 V vs. Ag/AgCl and an anodic potential of 0.35 V vs. Ag/AgCl, close to the gold dissolution onset. The cathodic pulse duration (ton) was fixed at 0.5 s, while the anodic pulse duration (toff) was varied from 0.5 s to 2.5 s to examine its influence on crystal growth. At the less negative cathodic potentials examined, potentiostatic electrodeposition and symmetric pulses (ton = toff = 0.5 s) produced poorly defined structures. Extending the anodic pulse duration promoted the formation of structures with tetrahexahedral and truncated bipyramidal geometries. At a cathodic potential of -0.45 V, potentiostatic electrodeposition formed gold octahedra, whereas asymmetric pulsing (toff > ton) induced a shape transition from octahedra to concave morphologies such as rhombic hexecontahedra and hexoctahedra. Lead underpotential deposition (Pb UPD) measurements on pulse-deposited gold indicated the presence of structures enclosing [n(110)×(hkl)] facets. Gold deposits with octahedral morphologies exhibited more intense (111) features in their Pb UPD response. To further probe the relationship between surface structure and electrocatalytic response, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) oxidation was investigated as a structure-sensitive model electrocatalytic reaction on pulse-deposited and potentiostatically deposited gold. Pulse-deposited gold structures exhibited lower onset potentials and higher activity for partial HMF oxidation. In contrast, potentiostatically deposited gold with a greater proportion of (111) domains exhibited higher current for the oxidation of the alcohol group in HMF. These results show that pulse electrodeposition is a valuable technique for tailoring surface geometries and highlight the effect of the DES electrolyte in inducing gold shaped structures.

item.title: Identifying Oxidation State Defects in Electrically Conductive Metal-Organic Frameworks via Solid-State NMR
item.description: Electrically conductive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have received significant attention for use in energy storage and gas sensing devices. Whilst their crystalline and tuneable structures have allowed for extensive investigation of the relationship between bulk MOF structure and performance, the exploration of molecular defects and how they may impact electrochemical properties remains limited. Here, we investigate oxidation-state defects in the prototypical two-dimensional layered framework Cu3(HHTP)2 (HHTP = 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene). Complementary 1H and 13C solid-state NMR experiments and paramagnetic chemical shift calculations allow us to identify co-existing metal and ligand oxidation-state defects, including a significant proportion (≥ 10%) of Cu+ / quinone-terminated HHTP defect sites. Importantly, we identify these defects in samples prepared using multiple literature methods. Cu3(HHTP)2 samples synthesised in the presence of oxidising agents contain a 30-50% higher concentration of Cu and HHTP oxidation-state defects. These samples exhibit substantially poorer electronic conductivity and energy storage capabilities, whilst their ability to sense H2S and SO2 gases is moderately improved. This work thus exposes the existence of defect sites across Cu3(HHTP)2 preparation methods and demonstrates significant performance variability caused by said defects. Our work highlights the efficacy of investigating paramagnetic properties of these materials via solid-state NMR, and opens the door to defect engineering to control properties in electrically conductive metal-organic frameworks.
