Checkmate for CHK2: Discovery of First-in-Class Covalent CHK2 Inhibitors with High Potency and Selectivity
item.description: Checkpoint kinase 2 (CHK2) is an important regulator of the DNA damage response. Despite considerable interest in CHK2 as a therapeutic target, our understanding of its biological functions and therapeutic potential remains constrained by the limited availability of potent and selective chemical probes. Existing non-covalent inhibitors often suffer from limited kinase selectivity, and selective covalent CHK2 inhibitors have not been reported. Here, we describe the covalent CHK2 inhibitor (R)-12b, which selectively targets Cys231 at the P3 position of the glycine-rich loop (P-loop). Structural studies reveal an unusual binding mode associated with marked conformational changes in the N-lobe of the kinase domain. (R)-12b exhibits nanomolar biochemical and cellular potency, excellent kinome-wide selectivity, and good in vitro metabolic stability. Together, these properties establish (R)-12b as a first-in-class selective covalent CHK2 inhibitor and a valuable chemical tool for interrogating CHK2 biology and further exploring its therapeutic potential.

item.title: From physics-informed machine learning to de-Occamising physics: the case of the currentmagnetisation hypothesis
item.description: Occam’s razor implies that a fundamental theory should describe diverse systems with few adjustable parameters. We test how far the current–magnetisation hypothesis (CMH), a microscopic description of the Orsted magnetic induction, must be enlarged to cover wires, dilute plasmas and molecules. That is, we attempt a de-Occamisation of CMH. After finding failures in the original formulation, two repairs define the new formulation, CMH-ML: an adaptive k rule removes density-dependent plasma suppression, and a curl of correlation potentials removes the divergent-energy 1/r field around bounded currents. The Cu-wire-refitted baseline, L0, gives a Biot–Savart-like dilute-plasma response but severely underestimates benzene NMR shifts. A three-scalar iteration, L1, misses the joint wire–NMR target; a learned-interior iteration, L2, and a nine-parameter reduced refit, L3, reach it. L0–L3 remain within a few percent of the Biot–Savart dilute-plasma response. Their graphene-nanoribbon fields differ strongly: L3 overshoots the near-ribbon benchmark, so L2 is retained provisionally for the final predictions. The wire and benzene fits and the dilute-plasma response therefore cannot separate L2 from L3; the near-ribbon field can, and so it is where the flexibility CMH requires remains to be settled.

item.title: Electric Field-Driven Transitions from Nonclassical to Classical Carbonyls
item.description: Effect of external oriented electric field (OEF) is studied on the chemical bonding of isolated and complexed CO molecules using Density Functional Theory (DFT). Our findings, discussed the course of blue-shift and red-shift during the application of parallel and anti- parallel OEFs, with respect to the C–O bond vector, in isolated and complexed CO molecules. We give answer to a question, ‘Why the influence of electric field is more prominent in causing the red-shift than the blue-shift?’, via the detailed discussion of involved donor-acceptor interactions. Moreover, it is shown with suitable case studies that OEF can switch between classical and nonclassical carbonyl complexes.

item.title: Toughening Metallo-supramolecular Polymer Networks Using Multivalent Stickers
item.description: Multivalent interactions are ubiquitous in biological systems, where high overall binding affinity can be achieved through the simultaneous association of multiple weak interactions. In synthetic polymer materials, multivalent interactions have emerged as a promising strategy for constructing dynamic networks with enhanced mechanical performance. However, how the valency of metal-ligand stickers, as distinct from their number, governs the structure and properties of dynamic polymer networks remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce multivalent stickers into poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) networks by linking adjacent 2,6-pyridinedicarboxamide (pdca) ligands through short diamine spacers. Compared with monovalent controls matched in sticker number or in ligand content, the multivalent networks form more closely spaced coordination domains, stay within the linear viscoelastic regime at higher strains, exhibit a more than twofold increase in stretchability and toughness, and retain their domain structure and properties after thermal reprocessing. Moreover, variation of the spacer linking adjacent ligands reveals that spacer geometry alters the structure of multivalent binding and consequently, the resulting network and mechanical properties. These findings demonstrate multivalent sticker design as an effective molecular strategy that is independent of sticker density for regulating metal-ligand interactions and provide new insights for the development of high-performance dynamic polymer materials.

item.title: Covalent Spin Delocalization in a Mixed-Valence Bimetallic Cluster
item.description: In mixed-valence (MV) systems, charge and spin distributions are typically coupled, making it challenging to establish localized MV charge alongside spatially extended spin density. Atomically precise metal clusters offer a promising solution owing to their richly tunable electronic structures, yet stabilizing unpaired electrons in these clusters remains difficult. Here we report a robust, open-shell Cu2Pd2 cluster in which low-valent Pd mediates covalent spin delocalization across a C–Cu–Pd–Pd motif while preserving a predominantly localized Cu(I)/Cu(II) MV configuration. This decoupled charge–spin architecture confers remarkable thermal and electrochemical stability while projecting unpaired spin density onto catalytically active sites. Using electrocatalytic nitrate reduction as a probe reaction, we demonstrate that this intrinsic spin topology enables selective activation of paramagnetic intermediates via spin-exchange, bypassing classical Sabatier scaling constraints to achieve a state-of-the-art ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 98%. Furthermore, external magnetic fields induce a volcano-like kinetic profile centered at 0.4 T and lower the apparent activation energy by 55%. This non-linear response rules out magnetohydrodynamic mass-transport effects and suggests a quantum spin-gating effect consistent with a proposed radical-pair mechanism, in which magnetic-field-induced Zeeman splitting modulates singlet–triplet mixing. This work establishes tailored spin topology and spin dynamics as an additional dimension for understanding and controlling chemical reactivity.

item.title: Decision-Tree-Guided Feasibility-Aware Bayesian Optimization for Materials Discovery
item.description: Material properties depend on composition, processing conditions, and other parameters that together define a vast design space. Exploring every possible combination is impractical because synthesis and processing experiments are expensive and time-consuming. Some candidates may also be unstable, form an undesired phase, or fail to synthesize. These outcomes create feasibility constraints that are not known before an experiment is performed. Here, we present a decision-tree-guided, feasibility-aware Bayesian optimization framework (DT-BO) for materials property optimization. A decision-tree classifier learns from the feasibility outcomes of previously tested candidates. It is updated periodically as new data become available. The classifier identifies regions that are likely to contain stable or synthesizable materials. A Gaussian process (GP) surrogate predicts the target material property given elemental and/or processing inputs. The acquisition function then searches primarily within the predicted feasible region to recommend the next candidate to consider. It also retains controlled global exploration to reduce the effect of classification errors caused by limited initial data. We evaluate DT-BO on three datasets : (1) synthetic dataset, (2) high-entropy alloy (HEA) dataset, and (3) hybrid organic–inorganic perovskite (HOIP) dataset. Across all three cases, DT-BO identifies high-performing feasible candidates more efficiently than conventional Bayesian optimization. The fitted decision trees also provide explicit if-then rules that describe predicted feasibility in terms of the input features. These results show that interpretable feasibility constraint learning can reduce unsuccessful experiments and accelerate materials design under initially unknown constraints.

item.title: Mining the cysteine-motif repertoire of airway mucins reveals redox-active mucolytic peptides
item.description: Muco-obstructive lung diseases are characterized by hyper concentrated airway mucus in which gel-forming mucins form mechanically reinforced polymer networks. Thiol-based mucolytics can reduce disulfide bonds within these networks, but clinically used monothiols show limited potency, whereas stronger reducing agents are constrained by instability and toxicity. Here, we systematically mined the major airway mucins MUC5B and MUC5AC for closely spaced cysteine motifs and screened the resulting mucin-derived peptide library for redox activity, oxidation stability, solubility, epithelial compatibility, and mucolytic activity. The identified Cys–[X]n–Cys peptides displayed pronounced sequence- and pH-dependent thioldisulfide exchange capabilities, with many peptides reacting faster than monothiol controls and several exhibiting reactivity approaching or superior to dithiothreitol (DTT). Reactivity was governed by the combined effects of thiol number, apparent thiol pKa, and local motif architecture rather than by a single physicochemical descriptor. Analysis of free-thiol stability and oxidation products further revealed sequence-dependent access to distinct intra- and intermolecular disulfide states. Together, these measurements provide a systematic sequence-redox framework for understanding how closely spaced cysteine motifs tune thioldisulfide exchange, with implications for the design of redox-active peptides and for understanding how local cysteine sequence environments may contribute to oxidative protein folding. Developability profiling identified soluble, reduced-thiol-stable, and epithelialcompatible candidates. Selected peptides reduced high-molecular-weight MUC5B multimers in cystic fibrosis mucus and MUC5AC multimers in asthma mucus, with activities in the range of DTT and greater than NAC under the tested conditions. These peptides were active in both pathological and healthy mucus, while showing compound-dependent differences in their concentration-response profiles across mucus environments. Our findings point at airway mucins as a source of redox-active peptide candidates with potential for mucolytic therapy and provide a broadly applicable resource for relating cysteine-motif sequence to disulfideexchange behavior.

item.title: Tracking the Biradical Evolution of Ozone
item.description: Ozone (O3) is a strongly correlated molecule of enduring interest in theoretical chemistry, whose ground-state multireference character is commonly characterized by configurationinteraction (CI) weights. However, preliminary experiments and related studies in this work show that such weights are not observables: two wavefunctions whose natural-orbital occupation numbers agree to within 0.015 nevertheless yield closed-shell weights that disagree when computed with different basis sets. To examine the relationship between the electronic structure and the geometric structure of ozone, this work employs gauge-invariant occupation-number descriptors together with the real-space unpaired-electron density, performing dense scans over the (r, θ) configurational space and classifying the distinct ways in which different geometric distortions influence the electronic structure.

item.title: Where Geometry Enters Molecular Generation: A Mathematical and Probabilistic Tutorial
item.description: Deep generative models are increasingly used to generate three-dimensional molecular structures, including molecular conformers, ligand poses, and protein backbones. Unlike generic point-cloud data, molecular structures occupy only a narrow, highly constrained region of three-dimensional Euclidean space determined by chemistry and physics. These constraints restrict the organization of atoms into molecular frameworks that have specific geometries. From the perspective of geometric deep learning [55], [56], molecular geometry is a source of prior knowledge that can be encoded as a form of inductive bias. This allows the model to incorporate known properties of molecular space, instead of learning them from data. Most reviews organize molecular generators by learning paradigm. Although this view is essential for understanding the training objectives and sampling algorithms, it does not explain where geometric inductive biases enter the generation process.

item.title: Lung cancer stem-like cells show no shared Raman signature of adipogenesis
item.description: Driving cancer stem-like cells into a terminal lineage is one strategy for differentiation therapy, and labelfree Raman spectroscopy is often proposed as a way to follow that conversion in single living cells. We reanalysed a public set of 214 single-cell Raman spectra from CD133+/CD44+/CD24- lung cancer stemlike cells of three non-small cell lung cancer patients, kept in adipogenic or control medium and measured after 7 and 14 days, comparing the two media only within one donor and one measurement session. Most of the fingerprint variance came from a single sharp-band component, X (bands at 680, 747, 952, 1143, 1338, 1449 and 1525 cm-1), which was present in both media, varied as one species (ρ = 0.96), was unrelated to the cells’ protein and C–H content (|ρ| ≤ 0.17), exceeded the phenylalanine band in 82% of cells and defined the first principal component of every pairwise model. After X was masked or subtracted, induced and control cells remained separable within some sessions, most robustly in one donor (balanced accuracy 0.66–0.80, permutation P ≤ 0.035). The direction of that difference, however, was not shared. Inter-donor correlations of the difference spectra (−0.55 to 0.40; mean −0.11) fell within a label-permutation null, a model trained on two donors classified the third at chance, and neither the ester carbonyl nor the CH2 stretching band showed a consistent lipid gain. A power simulation showed that a common signature as large as the observed within-session differences would have raised the mean inter-donor correlation to about 0.3 and been detected. The two time points were also stored on wavenumber axes 8–13 cm-1 apart. Over 14 days, adipogenic induction left no common Raman signature in these cells; the response was specific to each donor, and much of the spectral variance came from a component of unresolved origin.

item.title: Dynamic Modeling Framework to Predict Nanoemulsion Membrane Fouling Performance Under Constant Pressure, with an Exploratory Extension to Constant Flow Operation
Heat Quality Limits for Waste-Heat-Driven Direct Air Capture
item.description: With global climate targets increasingly at risk, rapidly scaling up direct air capture (DAC) is ever more important. However, the substantial thermal energy required for sorbent regeneration poses a major challenge by limiting its near-term carbon removal efficiency (CRE). Utilizing low-grade waste heat could alleviate this challenge, yet the temperature-dependent thermodynamic and kinetic penalties associated with low-temperature regeneration remain to be systematically quantified. Such quantification is essential to assess the potential to expand the range of viable waste-heat resources for DAC through lower-temperature regeneration and heat-pump-assisted upgrading. Here, we bridge the kinetic constraints of low-temperature regeneration in a heat-integrated contactor with system-level economics to map the feasibility of waste-heat-driven DAC across varying waste-heat temperatures. The contactor-level desorption model, fitted to experimental data obtained using saturated steam at 100 °C, was extended to 50–100 °C by incorporating the temperature dependence of intrinsic desorption kinetics. The resulting productivity model was integrated into a techno-economic framework considering both direct waste-heat utilization and heat-pump-assisted upgrading to map the minimum achievable levelized cost of capture as a function of waste-heat temperature. The analysis reveals that accounting for improvements in CRE extends the economically justifiable heat-pump temperature lift from approximately 35 °C on an energy-cost basis to 55 °C on a net CO2 removal basis. These findings define the economic feasibility envelope of waste-heat-driven DAC and demonstrate its potential to harness low-temperature waste heat where conventional heat recovery has limited economic viability, helping alleviate energy-related constraints on near-term DAC scale-up in today’s carbon-intensive energy systems.

item.title: Autonomous Bayesian Optimization in Electrochemical Aptamer Sensors
item.description: Electrochemical aptamer-based (EAB) sensors enable reagentless, real-time molecular detection, but their performance depends on square-wave voltammetry (SWV) parameters that are challenging to optimize due to the large number of possible parameter combinations. Conventional optimization studies in EAB sensing typically focus on sweeping the SWV frequency to identify operating conditions that maximize signal-on or signal-off responses to target molecules. However, this approach leaves the combined effects of frequency, amplitude, and step size largely unexplored. Furthermore, a single optimized parameter set is often applied across an entire batch of sensors without accounting for variations in electrode fabrication, morphology, and surface functionalization, each of which can influence the optimal operating conditions for individual sensors. Here, we implement an automated, closed-loop Bayesian optimization framework that tailors SWV frequency, amplitude, and step size to each individual sensor. Our approach efficiently explores the parameter space using a scoring function that rewards target-induced signal changes while penalizing measurement variability and noise. We demonstrate this framework using kanamycin-binding aptamers immobilized on planar and nanoporous gold electrodes and vancomycin-binding aptamers on nanoporous gold electrodes, identifying sensor-specific parameter combinations that optimize signal-on and signal-off responses. Notably, we find that amplitude and step size, in addition to frequency, influence the magnitude and direction of the target-induced response, potentially expanding the range of operating conditions available for kinetic differential measurement (KDM). We validate the optimized parameters through automated titrations, demonstrating improved sensing performance relative to a fixed reference SWV setting.

item.title: Structure-Based Design of Fungal Chitin Synthase Inhibitors: Targeting Catalytic Pockets and Translocation Channels
item.description: The limited treatment options for invasive fungal infections, together with the rise of antifungal resistance, have intensified the search for new drug targets. Chitin synthase (CHS) is an attractive antifungal target because it catalyzes the formation of chitin, a structural component of the fungal cell wall, and has no mammalian counterpart. The recent determination of high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structures of fungal and oomycete CHSs has provided a structural basis for structure-guided drug design. Drawing on the binding modes and structure–activity relationships of known inhibitors, this review examines strategies for designing new compounds that target either the cytosolic catalytic pocket or the transmembrane translocation channel of CHS. It further considers how computational biology and artificial intelligence could expand these approaches.

item.title: Deterministic Sub-100 µs Bare-Metal FPGA Spatial Voxel Screening and Dual-Target Structural Discovery of Allosteric TYK2 JH2 Inhibitors Selective Over JAK2
item.description: Selective allosteric inhibition of the tyrosine kinase 2 pseudokinase domain (TYK2 JH2) over the catalytic Janus kinase 2 domain (JAK2 JH1) avoids dose-limiting hematologic toxicities while treating autoimmune pathology. Here, we report a dual-target virtual screening and multi-seed consensus docking investigation comparing human TYK2 JH2 (PDB: 6NZP, 2.35 Å) against off-target catalytic JAK2 JH1 (PDB: 4IVA, 1.50 Å; 1.887 Å conserved binding-site Cα RMSD). From 2,500 unique chemical structures curated across ChEMBL 34, known JH2 controls, and structure-guided oral-window analogs, medicinal chemistry alert triage (PAINS, Brenk, NIH), physicochemical filtering (280 ≤ MW ≤ 490 Da), and hinge-binding pharmacophore matching retained 385 qualified 3D conformers. De novo SMILES redocking of clinical allosteric inhibitor deucravacitinib (BMS-986165) into 6NZP achieved ΔG = −8.733 kcal/mol (4.412 Å element-aware heavy-atom RMSD), while active-versus-decoy classification across known JH2 binders and clinical drug decoys achieved ROC-AUC = 0.867. Multi-seed AutoDock Vina consensus docking (seeds 42, 137, 2026) identified scaffold-hopped ChEMBL 34 leads including CHEMBL6914 (ΔGTYK2 = −10.72 ± 0.04 kcal/mol, ΔΔGTYK2-JAK2 = −1.11 kcal/mol, LLE = 3.05, Val690 = 3.34 Å, Lys642 = 2.86 Å) and CHEMBL266324 (ΔGTYK2 = −10.11 ± 0.12 kcal/mol, ΔΔG = −1.79 kcal/mol, QED = 0.654), alongside oral-window analog OIK-TYK2-003 (MW = 421.46 Da, LLE = 4.14, ΔGTYK2 = −8.84 ± 0.02 kcal/mol). Streaming 4,096-byte (16 × 16 × 16) pharmacophore grids via direct userspace PCIe Gen3 x16 BAR0 MMIO to a Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA (agfi-0b55f06c15a385187 on AWS EC2 f2.6xlarge) achieved 87.03 µs P50 (102.998 µs P99) latency, 0.25 KB constant O(1) on-chip state, and 100% bit-exact determinism at 9 W average (10 W max) VCCINT core power.

item.title: Thermodynamically Consistent Completion for Learned Initialization of Equation-Oriented Distillation Models
item.description: Equation-oriented (EO) simulation of distillation columns depends critically on the initial point given to the Newton solver. Learned surrogates and reuse of stored solutions are used as warm starts, but when they fail has not been quantified. Controlled experiments show that, at equal distance from the solution, starts that violate phase equilibrium fail three to seven times more often than consistent ones, and a local Newton analysis explains why: from a consistent start the first step is tangent to the manifold of the algebraic relations and contracts 10–40 times more strongly. We therefore propose a thermodynamically consistent completion. A surrogate predicts only the stage flows, liquid compositions and duties; bubble-point calculation, exact stream copying and explicit auxiliary relations then fill in every other variable so that all non-conservation constraints hold. The operator has no trainable parameters and takes 1.4–3.9 ms per column. On IDAES tray columns (binary NRTL, ternary BTX at 10 and 40 stages, a two-column recycle flowsheet, and real non-ideal mixtures of two to five components with up to 60 stages): • 10 stages: 99.5% convergence, against 94.2% and 81.4% for a network predicting the full variable vector, with less than half the iterations. • Recycle flowsheet: 99.4%, against 86.9% for nearest-neighbour reuse and 88.7% for the full-vector network. • 40 stages: 0.79, against 0.65 for nearest-neighbour reuse and 0.52 for the full-vector network. • Mean time to solution 1.8–24 times shorter in 15 of 16 comparisons; one network transfers to unseen column sizes (0.83–1.00 at 24–30 trays against 0.17–0.64 without completion). The benefit vanishes where convergence is governed by distance (an electrochemical cell) or by the phase-equilibrium formulation (near-azeotropic columns).

item.title: Different, but not too different: design rules for high-entropy molecular glasses
item.description: High-entropy mixtures of organic molecules can resist crystallization and form liquids as strong as silica, even when each component alone is a fragile glass former. Why this happens and how to design such mixtures has remained unclear. Here, closed-form expressions for their liquidus and eutectic show that freezing-point depression cannot be the whole story. Extending Adam–Gibbs theory to include mixing entropy gives a new expression for fragility in terms of measurable properties of the pure liquid, provided mixing entropy is not consumed on cooling. This accounts for the observed drop in fragility with component number in perylene mixtures although the record-low fragility values of slowly cooled mixtures lie below the prediction and require π-stacking. Thermodynamics and fragility then point to a design rule, that molecules must be different, but not too different. Molecules that are too alike crystallize as a solid solution and relax like a onecomponent liquid, whereas molecules that are too unlike phase separate. This provides a guide to the design of stable highentropy glasses, from amorphous drugs to organic electronics.

item.title: Evidence-Based Design and Verification of S-Scheme Heterojunctions for Solar-Driven Hydrogen Production: A Critical Review
item.description: A higher H2 evolution rate is often presented as evidence of an S-scheme pathway, yet it cannot establish the direction of interfacial charge transfer, and detecting H2 does not show that water was split. This critical review proposes a design–mechanism–reaction (D–M–R) framework that grades separately the design controls, the mechanism evidence and the reaction accounting of each study, and applies it to 32 purposively selected datasets from 2023–2026. Nineteen measure sacrificial H2 and four do not state the medium. Four report H2 and O2 from pure water within 10% of the stoichiometric electron balance, and only two report solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies (0.17% and 0.21%) under the required conditions. Seven use direction-reporting probes of two different observables, but none measures the direction under working conditions. A blinded second rater agrees within one level on every grade. Controls that vary one feature at a time and quantified electron balances are most needed.

item.title: Benchmarking Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials for Reactive Chemistry: Failure Modes in Nitromethane Decomposition
item.description: The failure modes of ab initio methods and empirical force fields are well documented, but those of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) in reactive chemistry remain largely uncharacterized. We benchmark five MLIPs on condensed-phase nitromethane decomposition against coupled-cluster dissociation energies and published simulations, and trace each model’s failure to a specific component: the global spin label of MACE-OMol-0 and UMA-S-1P1 produces a spurious ~25 kcal/mol rise as fragments separate, gaps in the training data of ANI-1xnr cause it to underbind dissociation into two polyatomic radicals by up to 48 kcal/mol, and the absence of close-contact configurations from the training data of MACE-OFF23 and MACEOsaka24 leads to unphysical energies at short interatomic distances, more severely in MACEOFF23. The responsible component determines the remedy: the spin-label artifact cannot be fixed within the models’ input format, the ANI-1xnr error is corrected to within 1 kcal/mol by physics-constrained data augmentation, and the short-range failure of MACE-OFF23 persists even with a standard screened nuclear repulsion term. Because corrected dissociation energies do not by themselves restore physical decomposition kinetics, we join recent calls to judge MLIPs by their failure modes and predicted observables rather than by aggregate energy and force errors.

item.title: Discovery and Characterization of an Aerobactin-like Lanthanide-Binding Metallophore in Methylobacterium mesophilicum
item.description: Lanthanide (Ln)-dependent methylotrophs have evolved specialized mechanisms for metal recognition and acquisition, yet the chemical diversity of small-molecule Ln-binding metallophores remains poorly understood. Here, we surveyed 214 Methylobacterium genomes and identified four major families of non-ribosomal peptide synthetase-independent metallophore biosynthetic gene clusters, revealing substantial unexplored diversity in putative metal-binding natural products. Investigation of an aerobactin-like cluster from the non-model methylotroph Methylobacterium mesophilicum A47 led to the discovery of Mesobactin, an amphiphilic citrate- and hydroxamate-containing metallophore bearing asymmetric fatty acyl substituents. High-resolution mass spectrometry, heterologous expression, and multidimensional NMR spectroscopy were used to establish the chemical structure of Mesobactin. Next, a modular synthesis of the symmetrical derivative sym-mesobactin was developed to interrogate Ln coordination. Mesobactin and related metabolites bind Fe³⁺, La³⁺, and Nd³⁺, with 1H NMR and native mass spectrometry supporting formation of a predominantly 1:1 La³⁺–sym-mesobactin complex. Competition with xylenol orange revealed concentration dependent La³⁺ binding, with competition observed when Mesobactin ligands were present in excess. Together, these findings identify an aerobactin-like scaffold for biological Ln coordination and expand the chemical and physicochemical landscape of Ln-binding metallophores beyond a model of high-affinity, freely soluble metal chelation.

item.title: Discerning the chemical individuality of alcoholic beverages with polymer-based fluorescence fingerprinting
item.description: Alcoholic beverages have distinctive chemical compositions shaped by raw materials and production histories, and this individuality is closely tied to regional cultures, traditions, and industries. Simple, objective methods for capturing this chemical individuality are important for quality control and for preserving product value. Here, we developed an analytical platform using an array of aggregation-induced emission (AIE) polymers bearing diverse functional groups to generate fluorescence fingerprints of brewed beverages, liqueurs, and distilled spirits. Statistical analysis of these fingerprints enabled highly accurate discrimination of sake, a traditional Japanese brewed beverage, by brand and production specifications, as well as of fruit-based liqueurs differing in source fruits and product specifications. The platform also tracked the temporal evolution of fluorescence fingerprints during sake storage. Importantly, distinctive fingerprints enabled discrimination among products of awamori, a traditional Japanese distilled spirit, despite the removal of many nonvolatile constituents during distillation. Furthermore, we demonstrated a simplified sensing format in which three polymers bearing different environment-sensitive fluorophores are mixed to obtain multichannel fluorescence responses from a single reaction vessel. These findings show that fluorescent polymers can capture the chemical individuality of diverse alcoholic beverage matrices composed predominantly of small molecules, opening possibilities for convenient product discrimination and quality-related fingerprint analysis.

item.title: Symmetry-breaking control of spin states in cobalt-metalated carbaporphyrinoid macrocycles
item.description: The on-surface synthesis of porphyrinoid-based nanostructures has recently emerged as a powerful approach to engineer functional molecular materials with atomic precision. Here, we demonstrate the control of spin states in low-coordinated metal centers through symmetry breaking in carbaporphyrinoid macrocycles. Asymmetric carbahemiporphyrazines, featuring a symmetry-broken coordination cavity compared to other hemiporphyrazine analogues, enable modulation of the electronic structure of the metal center. Surface-assisted [3+3] cycloaromatization of carbahemiporphyrazine precursors on Au(111) yields well-defined oligomeric architectures, which are structurally determined by scanning tunneling microscopy and non-contact atomic force microscopy. While symmetric cobalt-metalated dicarbahemiporphyrazines exhibit a spin S = 1⁄2, their asymmetric counterparts stabilize higher spin states (S = 3⁄2), as evidenced by scanning tunneling spectroscopy and supported by computational investigations. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy further reveals the competition between self-metalation with Au adatoms and cobalt incorporation in the carbahemiporphyrazine macrocycle, highlighting the role of the coordination environment and substrate in determining the metalation pathway and spin state. These findings demonstrate that symmetry breaking in hemiporphyrazines can be used to access higher spin states, providing fundamental insights into the coordination chemistry, reactivity, and electronic structure of non-aromatic phthalocyanine analogues.

item.title: Where Does the Fluorine Go? A Systematic Evidence Audit of Fluorine Fate and Carbon’s Role in PFAS Photocatalysis
item.description: Carbon-containing photocatalysts are proposed for treating per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), but performance is usually reported as parent-compound loss, which does not distinguish adsorption, transformation and C–F bond cleavage. We searched Scopus and Web of Science and audited 115 studies (121 experiments), coding fluorine in six measurable reservoirs and an unresolved fraction, recalculating defluorination and grading evidence for carbon’s electronic role. No study quantified fluorine in all reservoirs: 35 studies measured no fluoride, 12 extracted PFAS from the spent catalyst, one quantified catalyst-bound fluoride and none measured volatile products. Eight of nine numerical fluorine balances covered only the aqueous phase (42–93% recovery); the one including the catalyst recovered 2.35%. Removal exceeded defluorination by a median of 55.8 percentage points when removal included dark adsorption (n = 19) and by 10.4 points when degradation was reported (n = 11); the baseline was not stated for 33 of 63 paired values. Four of twelve recalculable defluorination values did not reproduce, one exceeding the theoretical maximum. The strongest evidence for carbon’s electronic role was correlative charge-carrier data in 67 studies and assertion, calculation or scavenger tests in 40; direct electron transfer to PFAS was shown for two intrinsically photoactive catalysts, neither compared with a carbon-free material. Sixty studies compared carbon-free or carbon-only materials, but none normalized performance to adsorbed PFAS. Carbon’s sorptive functions are well documented; its independent contribution to C–F activation in carbon-supported composites is untested. We propose a four-level reporting standard that separates removal, defluorination, fluorine closure and mechanistic claims.

item.title: Neurocosmetics: Active Ingredients, Transdermal Delivery and Evidence for Efficacy Claims
item.description: Neurocosmetics target cutaneous nerve receptors and the skin-brain axis, and have become a popular category in skincare in recent years. However, there are considerable controversies over efficacy evidence and the boundaries of product claims. Neuropeptide mimetics, TRP channel modulators, endocannabinoids, probiotics and postbiotics are the main active ingredients of such products. The transdermal delivery efficiency of macromolecular actives such as peptides is limited by the stratum corneum barrier. Nanocarriers, chemical penetration enhancers and matrix optimization are major transdermal strategies, yet these technologies face practical constraints in production and skin tolerance. Attention should be paid to skin irritation, sensitization, phototoxicity of aromatic components and inhalation risks during raw material application. A three-tier efficacy evidence framework reveals that most products only have evidence supporting local cutaneous effects but make claims related to central emotional regulation, resulting in mismatched evidence levels. In accordance with domestic cosmetic regulatory requirements, efficacy claims of neurocosmetics should be restricted to local skin physiological effects, and exaggerated psychological and emotional claims should be avoided.

item.title: Sequence-dependent structural propensities of low complexity peptides accessed by automated flow synthesis
item.description: Automated fast-flow peptide synthesis enabled milligram-scale access to 10 peptides designed with restricted sets of amino acids spanning three repeat architectures. Solid-state ATR-FTIR reveals heterogeneous β-turn and β-sheet signatures. AlphaFold 2 and 3 predictions reveal sequence-dependent agreement. Together, this pipeline realiby delineates structural propensities of peptides with low sequence complexity.

item.title: Multitask Neural Networks for Multi-Solvent Solubility Prediction: Joint Learning with Lipophilicity, Melting Point, and Hydration Free Energy
item.description: The accurate prediction of solute solubility (LogS) and related properties such as partition coefficient (LogP), melting point (MP), and hydration free energy (∆Ghyd) plays a vital role in molecular design and specifically drug discovery. Data-driven machine learning approaches have received considerable attention due to their ability to provide fast and accurate predictions. However, the scarcity of high-quality datasets poses a significant obstacle to their wide applications. One strategy to circumvent this challenge is to employ multitask (MT) models which allow sharing of information and exploitation of correlations across various tasks, thereby addressing the limitations in data for specific tasks. In this work, two MT algorithms based on neural networks and the multi-explanation graph attention network (MEGAN) were developed and used for the simultaneous prediction of 19 tasks comprising 16 datasets of LogS together with one dataset of each of LogP, MP, and ∆Ghyd as helping tasks. In addition, single-task (ST) versions of the aforementioned models together with four more models, namely graph attention networks, random forest regression, Gaussian process regression, and support vector regression were analyzed for comparative purposes. It was found that both MT-DNN and MT-MEGAN models trained on all 19 tasks on average outperform all the other models when comparing the mean R2 values, with MT-DNN additionally achieving the lowest weighted RMSE and enabling predictive performance even for datasets with fewer than 50 data points. However, for the individual tasks there was no consistent improvement of the MT models.

item.title: Nucleus-Independent Chemical Shifts in disordered nanoporous carbons are governed by the long-range magnetic response of the carbon framework
item.description: Nanoporous carbons are widely used in energy storage, gas storage, and separation technologies due to their high surface area, porosity, and electrical conductivity. Understanding atomic-scale structure is critical for interpreting performance, yet disorder greatly complicates characterization. NMR chemical shifts of adsorbed molecules have emerged as a probe of structural disorder, but how nucleus-independent chemical shifts (NICS) relate to structure in realistic, disordered carbons remains poorly understood. Here, we generate realistic nanoporous carbon structures using molecular dynamics simulations and compute pore-averaged NICS using density functional theory, reproducing experimentally observed negative values across commercial nanoporous carbons. We find a moderate correlation between sp2 domain area and NICS, indicating that domain size alone is a poor predictor of the observed shifts, while NICS value also weakly correlate with heteroatom content and 6-membered ring fraction. Instead, decomposing local shielding from non-local contributions shows that the framework's bulk magnetic susceptibility, which implicitly encodes domain size, packing arrangement and defects, dominates the pore-averaged response. These results reframe NICS as a reporter of the framework's collective magnetic susceptibility, rather a local probe of isolated aromatic environments. item.title: MDwizard: GUI software for interactive binding site analysis, MD simulation and physics-based residue mapping.
item.description: Post-docking analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and pharmacophore classification are commonly used methods in computational hit discovery. Although several open-source and commercial tools exist for each process, there is no single graphical user interface (GUI) which helps researchers navigate from post-docking analysis to classification of residues with MD. Moreover, MD simulation in Windows is usually implemented through docker which is impractical for novice users. To address this issue, we present MDwizard, a GUI with easy one-click installation for Windows and Linux. MDwizard includes interactive 3D and 2D protein-ligand (PL) interaction maps, surface/van der Waals visualisation along with sketching and docking. MD simulation setup is interactive, while trajectory/analysis plots are automated. Furthermore, MDwizard assists in classifying residues with dynamic interaction occupancy and per residue SMINA AD4 score contribution. Four case studies (EGFR, MAO-B, ABL1 and ERα) showcase the effectiveness of the platform. MDwizard can be downloaded from https://sourceforge.net/projects/mdwizard/.

item.title: Tuning the Electronic Structure of Open-Shell Nanographenes through Hydrogen Bonding
item.description: Hydrogen bonding enables the formation of various self-assembled molecular materials, but its potential in modulating the electronic properties through intermolecular coupling has been rarely addressed. Here, we demonstrate that hydrogen-bondmediated interactions can substantially modify the electronic structure of open-shell nanographenes without altering their radical character. We synthesize a hydroxy-functionalized diradical nanographene (2) on a metal surface and investigate its self-assembly into hydrogen-bonded chains and find that intermolecular hydrogen bonding leads to a reduction of the molecular electronic gap, primarily through a shift of the single occupied molecular orbital toward higher energies. The chemical structure of the nanographene is determined by scanning tunneling microscopy and non-contact atomic force microscopy, while the electronic properties are investigated by means of scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Complementary theoretical analysis reveals a covalent-like character of the intermolecular O–H···O bonds, due to the Nuclear Quantum Effects (NQEs) on hydrogen atoms at low temperatures, suggesting that the hydrogen bonds provide an electronic coupling pathway between neighbouring nanographenes. At the low experimental temperatures employed (≈ 4 K), the hydrogen-bonded protons can enter a deep-tunneling regime, potentially enabling proton delocalization between adjacent oxygen atoms. These results establish intermolecular hydrogen bonding as a means to tune the electronic structure of open-shell nanographenes and highlight proton quantum dynamics as a potentially important component of electronic coupling in hydrogen-bonded molecular assemblies.

item.title: Accelerating Scientific Discovery in the AI and Quantum Era: Opportunities and Challenges for Theory and Experiment in Ultrafast Science
item.description: The field of ultrafast science is evolving rapidly due to the development of new light sources and technologies that enable researchers to visualize the motion of electrons and nuclei in ways that previously could only be imagined. These advances are coupled with a rapid growth in theoretical methods, computational resources, and AI/ML capabilities that are catalyzing unprecedented understanding of electronic structure and dynamics in molecules and materials. The parallel developments in experimental and theoretical approaches represents a unique opportunity to bring together these complementary tools to enable a significant advance in understanding and control of ultrafast dynamic processes. Now is the time to seize unique opportunities at the interface of experiment and theory in ultrafast science, where integrated approaches can deliver predictive insight, guide measurement design, and uncover mechanistic principles that were previously inaccessible.

item.title: Revealing hidden dynamics in steady-state heterogeneous catalysis through photon-statistical spectroscopy
item.description: Collective dynamical organization regulates essential functions across living and engineered systems, from coordinating tissue development [1] and clearing mucus from airways [2] to synchronizing electrical power grids [3]. In heterogeneous catalysis, underpinning modern chemical manufacturing, experimentally established examples remain scarce, with self-sustained oscillations in CO oxidation as the archetypal example[4, 5]. Harnessing the temporal organization of chemical reactions enhances catalytic activity and chemoselectivity [6, 7], yet whether apparently steady catalytic reactions conceal more general forms of collective dynamical organization remains unresolved. Conventional characterization predominantly captures ensemble-and time-averaged responses, reinforcing theoretical descriptions based on steady-state approximations that leave such organization unaccounted for[8–10]. To access this hidden information, we introduce photonstatistical spectroscopy (PSS), which distinguishes fluctuations associated with catalytic processes from those expected from photon-counting noise[11, 12], revealing chemically specific dynamical information beyond conventional measurements. Applied to CO oxidation over Pt, PSS recovers known oscillatory behaviour [4, 5] while uncovering additional temporal organization in apparently featureless signals. Mechanistic analysis indicates preferential sensitivity to a reactive fraction of CO* at CO*–O* boundaries and identifies signatures of coupled, otherwise unobserved surface processes. We then apply PSS to ammonia synthesis over a commercial iron-based catalyst at 100 bar, resolving previously unobserved, chemically specific dynamical organization that persists even after macroscopic steady state is reached during 100 h of operation. Combining operando infrared and quick X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals dynamical contributions consistent with NHx* intermediates and changes in the local structure of the catalyst, demonstrating the applicability of PSS across spectroscopic techniques. Our findings reveal that macroscopic steady state does not preclude organized microscopic dynamics and establish a means of connecting this hidden temporal organization to reactive species and catalyst environments, opening new avenues for understanding and ultimately controlling catalytic function and, more broadly, nonequilibrium processes.

item.title: Dynamic Ligand Exchange Enables the Self-Assembly of Redox-Active Molecular Crystals
item.description: By investigating the chemical and electrochemical behavior of iron trihalides, which are promising low-cost, earth-abundant intercalation materials, we reveal that superconcentrated electrolytes drive the self-assembly of new coordination compounds that crystallize via a solvent-exchange mechanism. In acetonitrile (ACN)-based superconcentrated electrolytes, FeIIICl3 spontaneously recrystallizes into the mixed-valence [FeII(ACN)6][FeIIICl4]2 molecular crystal. Driving this crystallization is the ability of Fe(III) metallic centers to oxidize ACN into ClCH2CN and HCl, as demonstrated by NMR and mass spectrometry. This autocatalytic spontaneous reaction forms solvated Fe(II) centers self-assembling upon supersaturation with dissolved FeCl4

item.title: The temperature dependence of rate coefficients of barrierless neutral and ion–molecule reactions in the high–energy limit
item.description: Accurate modeling of chemical networks in planetary atmospheres and circumstellar envelopes requires temperature–dependent rate coefficients across broad thermal regimes. In this work, we present an analytical model for barrierless bimolecular reactions, encompassing both neutral–neutral and ion–molecule processes, designed to interpolate rate coefficients over extended temperature ranges. By coupling long–range attractive interaction potentials (Lennard–Jones and power–law electrostatic forms) with microcanonical density–of–states ratios for the intermediate complex, we derive analytical expressions that describe high-temperature kinetic data. The model is validated on the neutral reaction HC2 + SO2 → HC2O + SO and the ion–molecule C2H5OH+2 + C2H5OH → (C2H5)2OH+ + H2O.

item.title: Oxidative aging enhances the ice-nucleating activity of tire-wear particles
item.description: Microplastics are increasingly recognized as widespread atmospheric pollutants with the potential to influence cloud glaciation and climate. Tire-wear particles (TWPs) are a major source of airborne microplastics, yet the effects of environmental aging on their ice-nucleating properties remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the influence of oxidative aging by combining the characterization of environmentally collected TWPs with controlled ozone exposure of lab-made particles. TWPs collected directly behind a moving tire exhibited clear spectroscopic evidence of surface oxidation and initiated freezing at a median temperature, T1/2, of −11.61 °C. However, the contribution of oxidation to this enhanced activity could not be distinguished from that of inorganic material also present in the environmental samples. To investigate the role of oxidation, pristine lab-made TWPs were therefore exposed to ozone. This treatment reproduced key spectroscopic characteristics of the oxidized environmental particles and substantially enhanced the ice-nucleating activity. After 360 min of ozone exposure, T1/2 increased from −16.46 to −11.81 °C, with ice-nucleation site densities approaching those of K-feldspar. These findings suggest that oxidation of the tire material itself contributes to the enhanced ice-nucleating activity of the environmental TWPs. Accounting for aging-induced surface-chemistry changes will therefore be essential for assessing the atmospheric icenucleating potential of TWPs and understanding their possible contribution to cloud glaciation, precipitation and climate.

item.title: The ensemble dynamics of protein folding, the case of Trp-cage
item.description: Analyzing the complex trajectory of a folding protein is almost as challenging as generating it. In this work we show that the eigenfunctions and the eigenvalue of the dynamic operator are a powerful tool to analyze in a transparent and straightforward way the folding and unfolding dynamics of a protein. Use of the dynamics operator implies that we are not focusing on single trajectories but rather on the evolution of ensembles of system replica trajectories. We apply this approach to the study of Trpcage protein dynamics for which extensive unbiased molecular dynamics simulations are available. We find that, when projected on the lowest eigenfunctions, the simulation data lie on a low dimensional manifold. This facilitates the analysis and just from a visual inspection different intermediate states can be identified. From the eigenvalues we estimate folding and unfolding times in agreement with the experimental data. The transition from unfolded to folded state can take place either via a foldon mechanism or in a less probable manner via hydrophobic collapse. We use the generator eigenfunctions as a common basis for a range of stochastic analysis tools, including committors, mean first-passage times, and reactive currents. Together with the prediction of observable relaxation from different initial ensembles, these tools provide a practical framework for translating a learned dynamical operator into a unified description of the underlying dynamics.

item.title: Cleanroom-free fabrication of microelectrode arrays for Pb2+ stripping voltammetry in low-ionic-strength solutions
item.description: Trace metal contamination in drinking and natural waters remains a major environmental and public health concern, requiring sensitive and reliable monitoring tools capable of operating directly in the field. However, low ionic strength presents a significant challenge for electrochemical sensing due to increased solution resistance and reduced signal quality. Microelectrode arrays are well suited for electrochemical sensing in environmental samples. Their small size promotes radial or quasi-radial diffusion, enabling fast mass transport. Their low currents reduced ohmic drop and improved potential control, making them ideal for in situ and real-sample measurements. However, their fabrication relies on silicon technologies used in the cleanroom facilities. Gold microelectrode arrays of two different geometries (band and disc electrodes) were fabricated using a cleanroom-free approach. A dry film resist photolithography process is combined with digital mask UV exposure. Characterization results demonstrated good fabrication reproducibility across different batches and stable electrochemical performances. The fabricated microband electrode arrays were then evaluated for the detection of Pb2+ (over the concentration range 10–100 ppb) in a low ionic strength medium (3 mM), simulating real sample conditions. A linear response was obtained, and the limit of detection was estimated at 5.2 ppb, below the World Health Organization guideline value of 10 ppb for lead in drinking water.

item.title: An adaptive FP32/FP64 precision ladder for GPU-accelerated GFN2-xTB
item.description: Large-scale GFN2-xTB calculations spend most of their time in the dense eigensolver of the self-consistent-charge (SCC) iterations. On workstation and consumer GPUs, whose double-precision (FP64) throughput is a small fraction of their singleprecision (FP32) throughput, offloading this step in FP64 yields only a small speedup. We present an adaptive FP32/FP64 precision ladder for the GPU eigensolver of xtb: every SCF starts with FP32 solves, switches to FP64 once the largest change of the Hamiltonian diagonal falls below a threshold, and accepts a converged density only from an FP64 solve. The ladder is a small patch to xtb that leaves the CPU path bitidentical. For 32 test systems with up to 19,200 basis functions, single points above about 5000 basis functions run 2.4–3.8 times faster than on the CPU at 16 threads each, 1.9–3.2 times at 32 threads each and up to 6.6 times on a single thread, and the energies of all 29 systems that reach the GPU agree with the CPU results to within 2.4 × 10−7 Eh, below the SCC convergence threshold. In 20 ps of molecular dynamics the GPU run conserves energy as well as the CPU run, and a protein geometry optimization finishes 2.0 times faster.

item.title: New-to-nature Catalysis by Adaptive Protein Confinement in an Engineered Fatty Acid Photodecarboxylase
item.description: Engineering photoenzymes to perform new-to-nature reactions is a promising route towards green and sustainable photobiocatalysts. Fatty acid photodecarboxylases (FAPs) have been recently repurposed to catalyze radical cyclization reactions, but precise mechanistic information about how mutations redirect native activity is still lacking. Here, we combine QM/MM and ML/MM dynamic simulations to investigate the three key steps leading to cyclic products in a FAP mutant, previously engineered through directed-evolution techniques. We show that mutations enlarging the enzyme active site involve a delicate trade-off: they partially hinder the initial forward electron transfer, yet are simultaneously essential for enabling the subsequent cyclization step. Rather than statically pre-organizing the active site, the engineered enzyme adaptively confines the radical intermediate into distinct conformations at each step of catalysis, granting it access to productive cyclization pathways and achieving the experimentally observed ~90% cyclization yield. These findings establish adaptive confinement as a key determinant of new reactivity and provide a mechanistic framework for the rational engineering of next-generation photobiocatalysts.

item.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Low-Emission Methane Tri-Reforming: Carbon Formation, Hydrogen Production, and Operating-Window Optimization
item.description: Tri-reforming of methane (TRM) is a promising route for producing hydrogen-rich syngas while partially utilizing CO2, but its deployment is limited by trade-offs among methane conversion, syngas composition, reactor duty, and carbon deposition. In this study, a Gibbsequilibrium model in Aspen Plus was used to generate a database of 46,464 operating points spanning temperature, pressure, and inlet H2O/CH4, CO2/CH4, and O2/CH4 ratios. Decision tree, random forest, XGBoost, and artificial neural network models were trained and compared, followed by SHAP and permutation-importance analysis and multi-objective genetic-algorithm optimization. The neural network showed the best predictive performance. Explainability analysis identified temperature as the dominant factor governing carbon formation, followed by steam, carbon dioxide, and oxygen feed ratios. Optimization revealed multiple distinct operating windows, confirming that no single universal optimum exists and demonstrating a rapid, interpretable framework for low-emission TRM screening and design.

item.title: Operating Conditions Redefine MOF Design: Interpretable Windows Expose Cross-Process Conflict and Pressure-Driven Rank Reversal
item.description: High-throughput screening identifies which metal–organic framework (MOF) ranks highest under one set of conditions, but not whether its design logic survives another operating regime. Here, we discover compact descriptor windows across 278,407 ARC-MOF structures while jointly optimizing elite enrichment, support, and topology diversity. Under the reference three-component score definition, natural-gas and landfill-gas purification align closely (Spearman ρ = 0.949; top-decile Jaccard 54.37%), whereas post-combustion CO₂ capture and methane storage oppose one another (ρ = −0.812; Jaccard 0.15%). These correlation directions persist across tested score variants, while pre-combustion relationships are definition-sensitive. The reference scores yield 84 all-five top-decile structures (0.030% of the database), although the intersection varies under alternative definitions; 42 of the 45 with known topology are pcu. Single-gas CO₂ uptake rankings are conserved between 0.015 and 0.15 bar at 298 K (ρ = 0.947) but anticorrelated between 0.4 and 16 bar at 313 K (ρ = −0.395), with 27.5% of low-pressure elites in the latter comparison entering the high-pressure bottom decile. Descriptor association reversals are consistent with established affinity–capacity trade-offs, but do not independently identify a causal mechanism. Process-specific rule cards distinguish broad explanatory regions from narrow high-precision archive-labelled shortlists, and Pareto selection makes enrichment–support–topology trade-offs explicit. This framework converts database screening from a list of winners into explicit, operating-condition-specific screening guidance.

item.title: Shape, Size and Symmetry: What Sets the Root Count of the Spin-Adapted Coupled Cluster Doubles Equations
item.description: For a random Hamiltonian, the number of solutions of the spin-adapted coupled cluster doubles (CCD) equations depends only on the active-space shape. Molecules give fewer. Here, the effect of symmetry was separated from that of problem size. Twenty-seven closed-shell systems with up to 21 amplitudes were enumerated by homotopy continuation, alongside symmetry-averaged random Hamiltonians and subgroup chains at fixed orbital content. Where one occupied or one virtual orbital is active, CCD is an eigenvalue problem, and the number of isolated roots is dG + 1, with dG the number of totally symmetric doubles. At the nonlinear shape with 998 generic roots, axial symmetry leaves 24 isolated roots and spherical symmetry 6; the others form continua. Finite groups leave most roots isolated. C2v leaves 926 on four scaffolds with one C2v content, whereas D2d leaves 916 or 600 at two contents. The octahedral and tetrahedral groups produce continua without continuous symmetry of the equations. The count is therefore set by the group and the representation content of the active orbitals, not by size or group order. Every symmetric control reproduced its molecule’s count, except in one dimer structure with two roots beyond numerical reach. For BH, the CCD coefficients of the symmetric family span 17 of the 83 dimensions its monomial support allows. Breaking the symmetry restores the generic count discontinuously; the extra roots arrive from infinity. The smallest-norm real root is the ground state in every system, and other roots match excited singlets only for weakly coupled electron pairs.

item.title: Expanding the Toolbox for β-Fluoroamine Synthesis: Mechanistic and Stereochemical Insights into I(III)-Mediated Aminofluorination of Cinamyl Carbamates.
item.description: The aminofluorination of allyl carbamates represents a valuable strategy for the synthesis of β-fluoroamine scaffolds, which are of high interest in medicinal chemistry. In this study, we explore three complementary methodologies for this transformation: (i) direct aminofluorination using TolIF2, (ii) in situ generation of PhIF2 from PhIO and Base·HF complexes, and (iii) a sequential process involving aziridination followed by fluorine-induced ring-opening. Mechanistic insights were gained through experimental data, Hammett analysis, and DFT calculations. The direct TolIF2-mediated approach efficiently afforded fluoro-oxazolidinones with high syn selectivity, particularly for electron-poor substrates, while the in situ PhIF2 method proved less effective due to competing side reactions. The sequential strategy allowed for controlled access to either syn- or anti-diastereomers, depending on the fluorinating agent used, with DMPU·HF favoring anti-products and Et3N·HF leading to varying selectivity depending on substrate electronics. Mechanistic studies revealed the key role of HF clusters and hydrogen bonding in dictating stereoselectivity, with aziridine protonation serving as a crucial determinant of the reaction outcome. These findings provide a deeper understanding of aminofluorination strategies, enabling improved stereocontrol and expanding the synthetic potential of β-fluoroamine derivatives.

item.title: An untargeted total-variable approach for micro- and nanoplastics classification and quantitation using Py-GC/HRMS
item.description: Pyrolysis-GC/MS is widely used for quantifying micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in environmental and biological samples, yet its reliance on a small set of pre-selected indicator compounds introduces substantial risk of false positive identification, particularly in complex matrices where endogenous compounds can generate the same pyrolysis products. Here, we present a total-variable classification framework that leverages the full two-dimensional retention time × m/z spectral information from Py-GC/HRMS to identify polymers through their global fragmentation fingerprints rather than individual indicator ion. Twenty-two polymer standards were analyzed by untargeted Py-GC/HRMS and assembled into retention time × m/z intensity matrices (383 × 59,501; 0.01 m/z bins). After variance filtering (318 m/z channels retained) and principal component analysis (K = 3), samples were classified by elastic net regression, in which each signal is reconstructed from class-specific training dictionaries and assigned to the class with the smallest reconstruction residual. The model correctly classified 62 of 65 held-out test samples (95.4%). On an independent verification set of 12 samples (PA6, PHB and PS), 8 were correctly identified (66.7%). This work presents a proof-of-concept workflow that populates retention time × m/z matrices from Py-GC/HRMS data and identifies polymers by elastic net decomposition, offering a new perspective on processing microplastic Py-GC/MS signals.

item.title: Asymmetric Mechanical Deformation During Sodiation and Desodiation of O3-NaNi₁/₃Fe₁/₃Mn₁/₃O₂ Composite Cathodes
item.description: O-3 type layered metal oxides are promising cathodes for sodium-ion batteries due to their high theoretical capacity. They suffer from low-capacity retention associated with complex phase transitions and their brittle nature. However, there is not much known about how Na insertion and removal cause mechanical deformations in the composite cathode during cycling. Here, we synchronize operando strain and stress measurements with electrochemical analysis to capture the real-time deformation behavior of NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 cathodes during cycling. The operando mechanical measurements reveal nonmonotonic deformation of the NFM composite cathode during both charging and discharging. Strain rate analysis reveals that the intermediate deformation regimes do not retrace the charging sequence during discharge, demonstrating an asymmetric composite mechanical response. We provide an in-depth discussion about the possible mechanisms behind the distinct mechanical deformation stages in the NFM composite cathode. This correlation is critical to optimize the structure of the layered metal oxides for Na-ion batteries.

item.title: Host-sensitized lanthanide emission in Egyptian blue for shortwave-infrared bioimaging
item.description: Lanthanide ions emit sharp, photostable shortwave-infrared light but absorb weakly, so efficient sensitization remains a key challenge. Here we show that Cu2+, commonly a quencher of lanthanide luminescence, acts as a broadband, long-lived host sensitizer for Er3+ and Yb3+ in Egyptian blue (CaCuSi4O10) and related copper tetrasilicates (MCuSi4O10, M = Ca, Sr, Ba). Flame-spray-synthesized nanopigments reach quantum yields of 43% (Yb3+) and above 70% (Er3+), including 57% in the NIR-IIb with an exceptionally large Stokes shift of ~900 nm. Spectroscopy reveals Cu2+ centers adjacent to Er3+ that transfer almost completely from the relaxed 2B2g state, whereas distant centers transfer slowly, followed by near-unity Er3+ emission. Transfer efficiency decreases with increasing M-cation size (Ca ≫ Sr > Ba), providing a simple design rule. Because Er3+ remains excited for ~12 ms, transfer saturates at low photon flux, making these pigments most efficient under weak light such as ordinary room illumination. We demonstrate their potential in transcranial super-resolution angiography of mouse cerebral microcirculation, luminescence thermometry (2% K-1) and biocompatibility, establishing hostsensitized copper tetrasilicates as robust, earth-abundant shortwave-infrared emitters for bioimaging.

item.title: From Generic to Real: Symmetry-Induced Degeneracy in the Coupled Cluster Doubles Solution Landscape
item.description: The coupled cluster doubles (CCD) equations are coupled quadratic polynomials with many solutions besides the physical one. For generic Hamiltonians the number of isolated solutions is fixed by the active-space shape, yet real molecules have far fewer solutions, and the shortfall has lacked a structural explanation. This work presents a systematic protocol to quantify this gap and understand its origin. Six closed-shell hydrides, BeH−, BH, CH+, MgH−, AlH and SiH+, were enumerated at one spin-adapted shape of 21 amplitudes, alongside generic and symmetry-matched random Hamiltonians, by two independent homotopy routes. The generic system has 998 isolated solutions whereas every molecule has 24. The several hundred further endpoints lie on orbits of the rotation of the degenerate π pair, along which the correlation energy is constant, so the real solution set is not zero-dimensional. Isolated roots must be fixed points of the rotation, and a seven-variable system on the invariant subspace reproduces them one for one. Symmetry lowers the bound from 221 to 128 and no further; the reduction to 24 comes from the coupled cluster map, which confines the coefficients to a subvariety. The count is independent of the molecule, which enters only through the energetics.

item.title: The Importance of Iodine Oxides in the Initial Step of Nucleation: A Study on Hydration
item.description: The exact contribution of iodine-containing compounds in atmospheric new particle formation is still not fully understood due to ongoing debate about the initial steps of nucleation mechanism. Previous studies have proposed for both an iodine oxyacid-driven and an iodine oxide-driven nucleation. Furthermore, hydrolysis of the iodine oxides convert them into iodine oxoacids, potentially linking the two nucleation pathways. In this study, we investigate the hydrates of iodine oxyacid and iodine oxide clusters, and the hydrolysis kinetics of selected small oxide hydrates using quantum chemical calculations. The cluster configurations are sampled using the ABCluster program and the final structure and thermochemical parameters are calculated at the ωB97X-D3BJ/aug-cc-pVTZ-PP level of theory. The binding energies are further refined using a high level ZORA-DLPNO-CCSD(T0)/ma-def2-TZVPP calculation. We find that the iodine oxyacid clusters exhibit limited hydration, and their nucleation is slightly suppressed by hydration. Iodine oxide clusters often show substaintial hydration, which enhances their nulceation, with a maximum enhancement around 20–40% relative humidity (RH). Kinetic calculations suggest that iodine oxide hydrolysis may occur on atmospherically relevant timescales in larger clusters. Our findings suggest that iodine oxides might be important for the initial step of nucleation and subsequently are transformed into the oxyacids as the cluster grow.

item.title: The Limits of Library Scaling in Virtual Screening
item.description: Virtual screening libraries have expanded dramatically in recent years. Previous work has argued that screening larger libraries produces better experimental outcomes. This claim relies on two links: that larger libraries produce better scores, and that better scores produce better outcomes. In this study, we tested both. The first link shows rapidly diminishing returns: across six target-scoring function combinations, the score gains decreased as libraries grew even in log scale. The relationship was better described by a saturating power law than by the log-linear model previously reported. The second link is unreliable: a single chemical feature can markedly change the hit rate when the docking scores are similar. These findings suggest that increasing library size is not a reliable route to better experimental outcomes.

item.title: Learning Molecular Excitation Energies Beyond Local Atomic Environments
item.description: Electronic excitation governs photophysical processes in light-harvesting materials and photosensitizers. Designing these materials requires accurate predictions of excitation energies, but quantum-chemical calculations are costly for highthroughput screening. Geometric graph neural networks offer efficient alternatives. A prevailing strategy improves their accuracy through richer descriptions of local atomic geometry. However, local representations may miss molecularscale structural relationships relevant to excitation. Here we develop rEGNN-GT, combining equivariant local message passing with global self-attention to connect distant atomic regions directly. Across datasets spanning small molecules to organic semiconductors, rEGNN-GT outperforms its local equivariant counterpart, rEGNN, with comparable GPU memory requirements. It approaches the accuracy of DimeNet++, which explicitly encodes distances and angles, on small molecules. With over 60% less training GPU memory, rEGNN-GT matches DimeNet++ on conjugated chromophores and surpasses it on larger organic semiconductors. These findings highlight molecular-scale information exchange as a route to accurate, memory-efficient models of excited-state properties.

item.title: Exploring 2D and 3D Y2XT2 (X = C, N; T = O, F, Cl) MXenes for Optoelectronic Applications
Coupling Insoluble Pteroic Acid Using Quaternary Ammonium Salts: Synthesis of a Peptide Bearing a Folic Acid Moiety
item.description: Herein, I report a unique coupling method for insoluble pteroic acid. Tetraalkylammonium hydroxide effectively enabled solubilization, efficient coupling with an amine, and an easy workup process to produce folate-conjugated peptides. The generality and versatility were confirmed through coupling studies of several amino acids, demonstrating its applicability to the synthesis of various folate and pteroate conjugates.

item.title: Molecular dynamics and docking study of an illustrative VHH-like model at MICA α3 and small-molecule ENPP1 and EZH2 ligands
item.description: Some tumours evade natural killer (NK) cells by proteolytically cleaving the stress ligands MICA and MICB near the cell membrane within their α3 domains. Here I evaluated an illustrative, computationally constructed VHH-like model, VHH1, in complex with the isolated human MICA α3 domain (UniProt residues 182 to 274) using structure prediction, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD), and implicit-solvent rescoring, alongside small-molecule docking against two additional tumour immune-evasion targets, ENPP1 and EZH2. Across The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohorts in UALCAN (8,609 primary tumours and 738 unpaired normal tissue samples across 24 cohorts), median MICA transcript levels in tumours exceeded normal tissue medians in 13 of 24 cohorts overall, and in 9 of the 17 cohorts with more than five normal samples, while normal tissues also carried substantial baseline MICA RNA (medians 2.40 to 5.07 log2[TPM + 1]), indicating that bulk transcript levels alone do not establish tumour specificity. Sequence alignment confirmed that the human MICA and MICB α3 domains share 87 of 93 residues (93.5% identity), but MICB binding was not tested by docking or MD. AlphaFold 3 folded the individual VHH1 and MICA α3 domains with high confidence (chain pTM 0.87 and 0.85 to 0.86; n = 5 samples from seed 250104442), but the predicted complex had moderate global confidence (pTM 0.57 to 0.60) and low interface confidence (ipTM 0.13 to 0.22). Across three independent 100 ns MD simulations (2,001 frames per replicate), VHH1 remained internally folded (whole-run internal Cα RMSD 1.11 to 1.55 Å; domain-fitted Cα RMSF 0.67 to 0.72 Å) and retained contacts with the isolated MICA α3 domain in three distinct binding orientations. Replicates 1 and 3 maintained contact with four MICA α3 anchor residues (Ser193, Thr198, Gln228, and Arg247), whereas Replicate 2 shifted onto a lateral stalk surface involving framework region 3 residues; persistence in a pre-assembled complex does not prove binding affinity or shedding inhibition. Comparative single-trajectory OpenMM MM/GBSA estimates across 33 time-correlated frames per replicate (20 to 100 ns) were −49.1 ± 14.0, −20.2 ± 10.9, and −30.6 ± 5.0 kcal/mol for Replicates 1, 2, and 3, respectively. In AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 (n = 3 seeds per ligand), redocking the co-crystallised ligand TZV into human ENPP1 (PDB 6WEW) passed validation (top-pose RMSD 0.67 to 0.91 Å; best score −9.95 kcal/mol), although neither TZV nor the proposed model compounds Compound 1 (−9.10 kcal/mol) and Compound 2 (−10.32 kcal/mol) achieved inner-sphere Zn2+ coordination. Redocking S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) into human EZH2 (PDB 5HYN, chains A and D) failed validation (top-pose RMSD 7.78 to 7.86 Å) because Vina scored the crystal pose (−5.57 kcal/mol as-is; −7.05 kcal/mol after local minimisation) worse than alternative poses (−8.24 kcal/mol), rendering the tazemetostat docking result (−8.94 kcal/mol) strictly exploratory. All findings are unvalidated computational predictions that require experimental testing.

item.title: Before PFAS arrive: the native charge of the air–water interface sets trace PFOA adsorption and its response to salt
item.description: (PFAS) in unsaturated soils and their removal by foam fractionation, but how salt and pH change it at environmental concentrations (ng L−1 to µg L−1) is not established. The two descriptions in use were built from surface tension at mg L−1 and above. In one, adsorbed PFAS alone charge the interface, which predicts no salt effect at trace level. In the other, adsorption requires counter-ion pairing with a constant exponent, which predicts the same power law at every concentration. I show that neither carries to trace concentrations, and I develop a third description in which the bare air–water interface carries its own regulated negative charge and a trace PFAS anion responds only to its screened potential. The native charge is described by two closures, hydroxide bound to sparse sites and nanomolar surface-active impurities, with a screened image-charge correction. Calibrated on bubble zeta potentials alone (49 observations from five laboratories) and with one fitted constant for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), the hydroxide closure describes column transport coefficients with AICc 14.3 to 17.0, against 20.3 for self-charging and 109 for mass action, and predicts without refitting the higher adsorption at lower pH. A single fitted surface charge accounts for the eight-fold rise of PFOA adsorption on foam bubbles between 0.5 and 10 mM NaCl. Against eight adsorption coefficients from four further studies it gives a log correlation of 0.82 and a typical error of a factor of 3.1. The largest misses are all on one side: at about 0.1 M salt, with calcium at high coverage, and with co-surfactants, three independent methods place PFOA adsorption above the ceiling that any negative interface allows. I state predictions for a bubble experiment at two pH values that separates the descriptions and the two closures.

item.title: Can Helix Stapling Tune CISS? Bipyridyl-Stapled Peptides in Spin-Dependent Transport
item.description: Electron transport through chiral molecular systems can give rise to chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS), manifested as spin-dependent currents upon charge injection from magnetized substrates in the helical molecule. Although CISS has increasingly been interpreted as an interface-dominated phenomenon, molecular properties such as helicity (helical chirality) and electronic structure remain critical parameters influencing spin-selective charge transport. Here, we investigate how side-chain modification of helical peptides affects CISS by introducing an i→i+7 staple based on a planar aromatic 2,2′-bipyridine (bpy) linker into an alanine-rich 21-mer α-helical sequence. While circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy confirms preservation of helicity upon stapling, electronic structure analysis with time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) reveals that bpy significantly alters the optical properties of the helical peptide. Furthermore, scanning tunnelling microscopy showed pronounced aggregation/clustering in samples of the stapled peptides, induced by bpy-linker. On the other hand, the I–V curves demonstrated a tendency toward a larger current difference between the two magnetization states for the unstapled peptides compared with the stapled ones.
