item.title: Nonempirical Double-hybrid Functionals Entering the AI Field: the Adaptative LS1DH model
item.description: We introduce a machine-learning-assisted nonempirical double-hybrid density-functional approximation, dubbed adaptative LS1DH or aLS1DH, which combines the theoretical constraints of the linearly scaled one-parameter double-hybrid (LS1DH) model with system-specific flexibility. Based on kernel ridge regression (KRR) and convolutional many-body distribution function (cMBDF) representations, aLS1DH predicts optimal system-dependent fractions of nonlocal exchange and correlation while preserving size consistency. Its performance is assessed on the extended GMTKN55 and on the recently developed CYCLO70. The aLS1DH model consistently improves upon its parent functional, PBE0-DH, rivaling the latest machine-learning-based functionals such as skala functional. These results highlight the potential of machine learning to improve the accuracy of nonempirical double hybrids while retaining their underlying theoretical constraints.

item.title: Chemistry decides the calibration unit: five direct and one water-mediated interaction class
item.description: Typed protein–ligand contact models predict which interactions form, but they return point probabilities, not a statement of how often the true contact is included. We formulate per-atom, multi-label interaction sets for five direct contact classes (H-bond, hydrophobic, π, salt, halogen) and add water as a sixth, water-mediated class. Using cross-conformal calibration and conformal risk control on 750 crystal complexes across 29 targets, we show that the calibration unit is a chemical decision rather than a statistical default. At the 90% nominal level a chemistry-aware nonconformity score reduces set size by 7.9% (target-held-out) and 13.2% (scaffold-held-out), changing coverage by only +0.6/−0.6 percentage points. Per-type risk control attains false-negative rates of 0.096/0.079 at a 10% target, but only for classes with enough calibration positives: salt has 42 positives and is not estimable, while π is under-covered by a global threshold. Water is abundant (1,258 positives; 5.4% of ligand heavy atoms; 72% of complexes) and target-specific. A global threshold on the probability score leaves water at 0.905/0.937/0.931/0.853 coverage on target/scaffold/temporal/strict splits, but the original chemistry-aware score is water-blind by construction and drops to 0.735/0.751/0.750/0.635. Making the partner term water-aware recovers only 0.848/0.877/0.886/0.787, while per-type control gives 0.923/0.937/0.928/0.857. Per-type control is therefore not a universal winner: it fixes π and water, can lower halogen, and cannot estimate salt. The calibration unit should follow the chemistry of the class, not an aggregate coverage target.

item.title: When Nondetects Decide the Verdict: Left-Censored Data Handling and Compliance Decision Errors under Extreme Censoring
item.description: Compliance assessments commonly replace nondetects with zero, half, or the full reporting limit. We asked how often this choice, not the data, determines whether a 95th percentile (P95) or mean exceeds a regulatory limit. In a pre-specified simulation spanning 20–99% nondetects, structural zeros, and 30–1000 samples, we evaluated decision errors of substitution, nonparametric, censored-likelihood, and Bayesian methods. With one reporting limit, lower- and upper-bound substitution rarely disagreed at ≤80% nondetects but in 53–61% of data sets at 95% when the reporting limit exceeded the regulatory limit. In a screening reanalysis of the Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), substitution alone determined whether 458 PFOA and 406 PFOS systems were classified as exceeding maximum contaminant levels at the reporting limit. In simulations of this case, lower-bound substitution missed exceedances despite more sampling. In exploratory analyses, no eligible method kept both error rates ≤20% with 30 samples for most nondetect proportions. For upper-limit decisions, the best method needed roughly 300–400 samples at ≤95% nondetects, largely reflecting the narrow decision margin, and none sufficed with up to 1000 at 99%. Under extreme censoring, data often cannot identify the decision. The remedy is more samples or lower reporting limits, not a better estimator.

item.title: Downstream purification route influences the viscoelastic properties of silk-elastin-like polypeptide hydrogels
item.description: The development of novel recombinant protein-based materials requires a bottom-up understanding of sequence-processing-property relationships. However, most studies have focused on how the amino acid sequence determines material properties, whereas the effect of downstream purification (DSP) remains largely unexplored. Here, we compare two silk-elastin-like polypeptides (SELPs) with different molecular weight (MW) and clustering of silk-like blocks. Each SELP was purified by two different DSP routes: inverse temperature cycling (ITC) or ammonium sulfate precipitation (ASP). Using a combination of experiments and molecular simulations, we show that the DSP route affects hydrogel formation and viscoelastic properties in a sequence-dependent manner. The low MW SELP was insensitive to the DSP route, whereas ITC of high MW SELPs led to irreversible hydrogel formation and with a 2-fold higher storage modulus than ASP. Our multiscale characterisation suggested that DSP influences how readily silk-like blocks form intermolecular βsheet crosslinks as a function of the DSP route. These results indicate that SELP hydrogel properties can be modulated not only by sequence design, but also through the DSP route applied, which has implications on cost and efficiency for designing scalable SELP biomanufacturing processes.
